en: The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Equal Accumulation of All Virtues, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Mahāvana Kuṭāgāra Śālā in Vaiśālī.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus—ten thousand in number—all of whom were fully trained in the precepts, possessed of complete understanding, and attained to noble penetration.

There were also twenty thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom were non-retrogressive, had attained the various dhāraṇīs, and possessed unimpeded eloquence. They had all acquired supernormal powers, analytical discernment, and thorough comprehension; they were firm and steadfast in their mental concentration, conduct, and the movements of their minds, and they harbored wisdom and skillful means to cross over to the other shore. Their names were as follows:

The Bodhisattva Manas-cārin, the Bodhisattva Śubhamati, the Bodhisattva Uttaramati, the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīmati, the Bodhisattva Vardhamānamati, the Bodhisattva Vajramati, the Bodhisattva Anantamati, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, and the Bodhisattva Śaṅkhinī.
Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and fourteen thousand sons of gods also all came to the assembly.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of beings as he preached the sutra; desiring to relinquish his life-force, he declared that in three months he would enter parinirvāṇa.
The Bodhisattva Guṅso immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes so as to bare his right shoulder, knelt with his hands joined in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How profound! How marvelous!"
The Tathāgata wishes to relinquish his life-span and intends to enter parinirvāṇa in three months.
World-Honored One!

Please speak only of the protection of bodhisattvas, the rescue and gathering-in of bodhisattvas, that which is spoken by bodhisattvas, that which is manifested by bodhisattvas, and the planting of the roots of all virtues by bodhisattvas—how they do not sever the Buddha-teaching and sustain the Eye of the Dharma; how they bestow grace upon the noble assembly and do not abandon sentient beings, preaching the Dharma for them so that they may transcend to the path of the unconditioned.

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma’s grace will spread widely; Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas shall not abandon the unsurpassed, truly correct Way, never being separated from the Buddha. Listening to the sutras and making offerings to the Sangha, they establish their essential resolve; their minds are firm as they follow the Dharma and disperse worldly attachments. Whatever their thoughts turn toward, there is nothing they do not realize and penetrate; they embody the ultimate destination and excel in many ways. They constantly harbor a sense of shame and self-reproach, purifying themselves so as to remain free from transgression. Their reflections are noble and their deportment is complete; they are courageous in what they undertake, subduing toil and defilement. Having suppressed the stains of desire, they have no fear or hesitation; they move among the assemblies without dread or difficulty, and the hairs on their bodies do not stand on end.
O Heaven among Heavens!

How does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva advance and increase all virtues without lacking wisdom, without deviating from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and without ever failing or abandoning the aspiration for the Way?
With an inner nature that is magnanimous and resolute, they form friendships that lead ultimately to extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
In his conduct, his words and deeds were in perfect accord; the Buddha-dharma he followed was free from error or falsehood.
He constantly guarded the right precepts and remained unconfused regarding what he had heard. He maintained the three pure prohibitions and esteemed patience;

in every action toward the common people, he practiced equanimity, devoid of violence or arrogance. He skillfully cultivated diligence with a mind free from weariness or indolence in all that was required.
Accomplishing all deeds, practicing meditation with a single-minded focus and a serene mind, thoroughly understanding all meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and their manifestations,
establishing the will in wisdom and remaining free from the sixty-two views and doubts,
being clear, proficient, and masterful in all scriptures, and acting to rescue and sustain others by practicing the four debts of gratitude to provide vast protection— such is the state of a deva.

Superiorly, they delight in worldly seclusion and constantly contemplate impermanence; their minds dwell upon the various supernormal knowledges like the threshold of a gate, and their thoughts harbor no longing for the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

They brilliantly expound the Dharma teachings to subdue Māra’s enmity and all external paths, mindful of proclaiming the transformative influence taught by the Dharma King, and they revere and follow the instructions of the Dharma without seeking [anything else].
O devas and humans, as taught by the Buddha, one should take the Dharma as one’s vocation.

Without craving for food or clothing and free from lustful desires, one should extensively deliver all beings, releasing them from resentment and hatred; one should have compassion for all living things to eliminate ignorance and folly, and remain untainted by any dharmas or the dust of Māra. One should practice skillful means and the wisdom of the boundless, universally exhorting others.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa (translated into Chinese as Gouluo Lishi):
"Excellent, excellent!
You have great compassion and provide great peace and security; out of pity for the devas and the people of the world, you have questioned the Tathāgata on such a matter."
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well!
I shall now explain for you the extraordinary and immeasurable virtues practiced by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas.
The Bodhisattva Śṛṅkhalā addressed the Buddha,
saying, “I wish and desire to hear it.
The Bodhisattva Śṛṅkhalā and the entire assembly received the instruction and listened.

The Buddha said: "There is a samādhi named 'Equal Gathering of All Virtues. If a bodhisattva attains this concentration, their manifold virtues will increase and advance; they will not lack wisdom nor deviate from dhyāna-concentration. Their aspiration for the Way will never be deficient or abandoned, and their resolute nature will never depart from the Buddha. They will constantly hear the sūtras and dharmas, make offerings to the holy assembly, and practice the four debts of gratitude. Having done so, they do not forsake sentient beings."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Samādhi of the Equal Accumulation of All Virtues and proclaimed its name, remaining silent and without further speech.
At that moment, in the great city of Vaiśālī, there was a powerful wrestler named Vimalakīrti (in the Jin language, "Stainless Majesty"), who thought to himself:

"I am a wrestler; in this world, my strength and power are so formidable that there is no peer to me. Yet I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama possesses immeasurable and fierce power, his might being so towering that it is said to total ten types, and that his bodily joints are like a chain of hooks, through which he attains mastery."
"I wish to go and test him, to observe his way and see who among us excels.

Having thought this, he immediately departed from the city of Vaiśālī and went to the Mahāvana-kūṭāgāra-śālā to visit the World-Honored One. There he saw the Tathāgata surrounded by a retinue of countless hundreds of thousands, preaching the sutras. He illuminated the great assembly like Mount Sumeru rising majestically above the vast ocean; beholding his majestic countenance and divine radiance, his heart leaped with joy beyond measure. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the Mallas, wishing to cure and remove the defilements of pride, arrogance, and self-will, addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"I recall that in the past, when I was a Bodhisattva, my brothers and I competed in archery; where the arrow landed, you now take it up, for the Śākya maiden Gopī wishes to use it."
Maudgalyāyana replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
At that time, I did not see where the arrow had gone.”
The Buddha emitted light from his right palm, and the light illuminated the trichiliocosm; it pierced through the Iron Mountains and the Great Iron Ring Mountains that encircle this buddha-field.
Maudgalyāyana followed the light and saw the location of the arrow.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Do you see the arrow?"
He replied, "I have seen it!
And he further told him:
"Go and fetch the arrow.

Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana manifested his supernormal powers such that no one in the entire assembly failed to see it. In the mere time it takes a valiant warrior to bend and extend his arm, he reached the Great Iron Ring Mountains in an instant, intending to extract the Buddha’s arrow; yet while the trichiliocosm shook all over, the arrow did not move.
All those present in the assembly—the devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, Śakra, and Brahmā Kings—were without exception struck with solemn awe.
Ānanda adjusted his robes, knelt down, and asked the Buddha:
"For what reason does the earth shake, causing the entire world to tremble with fear?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Recall how in the distant past I drew my bow and released an arrow that pierced through Mount Tai;
when I sent Maudgalyāyana to retrieve it, he exhausted all his supernatural powers yet could not pull the arrow out, and even though the trichiliocosm shook for his sake, he was unable to obtain it."
Ānanda petitioned, saying,
"I pray that you will deign to extend your venerable aid.
The Buddha immediately granted his consent and aided him with the power of the Way.
Then, following the holy command, he grasped and pulled out the arrow, returning it to the Buddha.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, when you were a bodhisattva, how did you draw the bow and release the arrow so that it pierced through the iron mountain? Was it by the power of your parents, or by the power of your supernormal faculties?"
The Buddha told him:
"This was the power of his parents, not the power of my spiritual majesty (*ṛddhi*).
Had I employed my spiritual power, that arrow would have reached immeasurable and limitless worlds of Buddhas."
Maudgalyāyana asked again:

"How is it that a bodhisattva, by the power of his parents, can shoot an arrow so that it enters Mount Cakravāḍa; yet by the power of the Way and the merit of his own virtue, he can assist in gathering [beings] together? What may be used as a metaphor for this?"
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"The strength of ten ordinary elephants is not equal to the strength of one noble elephant;
the strength of ten noble elephants is not equal to the strength of one dragon-elephant (nāga-hastin)."
The strength of ten dragon-elephants is not equal to the strength of one great elephant;
the strength of ten great elephants is not equal to the strength of one skillful elephant;
the strength of ten skillful elephants is not equal to the strength of one blue elephant.
The strength of ten blue elephants is not equal to the strength of one *pṛṣata* elephant;
the strength of a hundred *pṛṣata* elephants is not equal to the strength of one minister-elephant;
the strength of a hundred minister-elephants is not equal to the strength of one athlete.
The strength of one hundred common strongmen is not equal to the strength of one great strongman;
the strength of one hundred great strongmen is not equal to the strength of one superior strongman;
the strength of one hundred superior strongmen is not equal to the strength of one half-chain strongman.
The strength of one hundred and fifty *kūṭadhāra* warriors does not equal the strength of one *saṃpūrṇa* warrior;
the strength of one hundred *saṃpūrṇa* warriors does not equal the strength of one *mahākūṭadhāra* warrior;
and the strength of one hundred *mahākūṭadhāra* warriors does not equal the strength of a single Bodhisattva who has attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
The power of a hundred Bodhisattvas who have attained patience (*kṣānti*) does not equal the power of a single Bodhisattva who has reached the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhāgata*);

the power of a hundred Bodhisattvas who have reached the ultimate stage does not equal the power of the merit of a Bodhisattva in his final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*), who, immediately upon being born and falling to the ground, takes seven steps.
The Buddha said, “Maudgalyāyana!

In the worlds of other directions, where the present Buddhas have established their lands and which serve as the dwelling places for perfected Bodhisattvas, when one has just been born and taken seven steps upon the ground, the earth extends downward for six million eight hundred thousand yojanas; having reached this depth, one finally encounters the water element.”

Each and every drop of water was distinguished as being like the bowl of a carriage; reaching upward as far as the Brahma Heaven, they sustained the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power out of compassion for sentient beings. The world was not diminished, nor was it afflicted or harmed; such was the ultimate, towering majesty of the Bodhisattva’s spiritual power.
The power of a bodhisattva at the tenth stage of ultimate perfection does not equal the power of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
this is what is called the power of the World-Honored One’s father and mother.
Furthermore, the predictions received by bodhisattvas based on the roots of virtue from their past lives are not produced through the power of transformations via the way of supernatural faculties.

Suppose a bodhisattva, by the power of their merit and the manifestation of spiritual transformations, proceeds to the site of enlightenment and sits beneath the Bodhi tree; then, by the power of their supernormal faculties, they lift worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with a single toe and first places them before their eyes in various other immeasurable and limitless Buddha-lands, yet without causing any harm or disturbance to the sentient beings therein—this is the bodhisattva’s power of spiritual transformation through the strength of a single toe.
The power of the Tathāgata’s supernormal transformations exceeds even this, being immeasurable, infinite, and inconceivable.

Even if the Tathāgata were to universally manifest all his miraculous powers, you would still be unable to believe them; how much less so could those of external arts, various heresies, and heterodox studies?
"Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!

When a bodhisattva goes beneath the tree of enlightenment, he gathers the four great elements and establishes them as a single element; having established this single element within the world, there is neither increase nor decrease."

At that time, Māra the Evil One went to the site of enlightenment accompanied by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of fierce and unruly followers; the Tathāgata immediately subdued and overcame them all.
What constitutes this oneness?
It is the power of equanimity.
Possessing the ten powers, he constantly applies great compassion and pity to all sentient beings, never harming or offending them.
What are the ten powers?
There are places that are limited and places that are unlimited; he knows these as they truly are.
He knows the past, future, and present as they truly are.
With single-mindedness, they enter the gate of liberation through meditative concentration and right reception, knowing them as they truly are.
They see the various differences among the faculties of all people, knowing them as they truly are.
They perceive the thoughts and intentions in the minds of other sentient beings, knowing them as they truly are.
He thoroughly and completely knows various kinds of bodies and innumerable forms.
He thoroughly and completely knows the conduct of the multitude, how their actions differ in being either good or foul.

With the eye of the Path, he perceives clearly from beginning to end the destinations of beings: how they pass away here and are born there, or pass away there and are born here; their names, clans, parents, and siblings; and how they commit evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, slandering the noble ones with perverted and false views, ultimately falling into the evil realms;

or how they perform good deeds of body, speech, and mind, not slandering the noble ones, possessing right view and following it in accordance, ultimately ascending to the auspicious realms—knowing all this as if examining it directly.

With the ear of the Way, one hears of heaven, the world, hell, hungry ghosts, flying insects, crawling creatures, and wriggling breathers; throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, even such vocal sounds are neither audible nor attached to, as one knows them through thorough investigation.

With his mind, he beholds the ultimate origin of all five destinies; his outflows are exhausted and free from defilement; beginning and end are entirely severed; his spirit is true and he is sagely realized; having understood the source of name-and-form, he knows it with thorough scrutiny.
These are the ten powers.
The power of the Tathāgata further transcends these and is inconceivable, penetrating throughout the ten directions without past, future, or present.

Thereupon, the Malla Vigatarajas, having heard from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, of these parental powers of the Bodhisattva, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness at such an unprecedented marvel. A virtuous mind arose within him, and he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Now, as I listen to what the World-Honored One has taught, by the power of my parents when I was a bodhisattva and by the ten powers, I cast aside arrogance, pride, and self-importance; I take refuge in the Triple Gem and vow to give rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, out of compassion for sentient beings so that they may attain great peace."
"Alas! May I attain the ten kinds of powers, just as the God among Gods possesses them, complete and without difference.

When the great assembly heard these vast and extensive vows of the Malla, ten thousand people resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and simultaneously raised their voices in song and praise, saying:
"May we by good fortune attain the power of the Path!"
"He is also like the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Saṃghāṭa addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"O Great Sage, for what reason do you now praise the Samādhi of the Equal Accumulation of All Virtues and then remain silent?"

I only pray that the Tathāgata will analyze and expound upon this samādhi that gathers all virtues, proclaiming the various practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so that those who have resolved their minds may attain this samādhi.
The Buddha told the Mallas:
"A bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path should receive the honored concentration. Why is this so?"
If one who has first resolved their mind upholds this honored samādhi, they will immediately possess universal entry into all virtuous qualities.
For example, O Great Strength!

Just as the currents of streams, springs, rivers, and great flows all return to the ocean, so too do the merits planted through giving and maintaining the precepts, the practice of equanimity, the wisdom of the Path, all tainted and untainted worldly deeds that transcend the world, and the blessings established among devas and humans—all these come to converge and flow into the conduct of a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind.
Therefore, sons and daughters of good family who wish to encompass all blessings should resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

It is like Mount Sumeru, the Iron Ring Mountains, the Snowy Mountains, and the Black Mountains; the various medicinal herbs, grasses, and other forests; the continents, great nations, provinces, districts, and towns; and the sun and moon that circulate and illuminate the four continents—all these are contained within the trichiliocosm.
Thus it is, O Malla!

Whether it be the tracks of ordinary worldlings, the unattached pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattvas who have attained rest and benefit, or the virtues of the Tathāgata, the Great Sage—for those who have first resolved to become bodhisattvas, they all gain access to this merit and blessing.
"For this reason, you should form this contemplation: if one gives rise to the aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, then one fully encompasses all virtues!
The Buddha told the Malla:

"It is like the various classes of living beings throughout the four quarters; the Wheel-Turning Sage King dwells as their sovereign, his merit and fortune being preeminent, and he governs the multitudes of people across the four continents."

May their merit be equal to the virtue of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin) without any difference. Let these vast and sublime merits be combined into the merit of a single Sage King. May the merit of every sentient being in the trichiliocosm be equal to that of a Wheel-Turning Sage King; then, let each such Sage King have twice the number of beings in the trichiliocosm, and let the sum of all these merits constitute the merit of a single person.

If all the inhabitants of as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were each to attain a fortune equal to that of this one person, what do you think, O Saṃgharakṣita? What would you call such a state?
"How could one possibly measure this merit?
Ghoṣila replied, "Yes,
O God among Gods!"
"The merit of a noble wheel-turning monarch is inconceivable; how much more so the merit of all those who have set their minds upon enlightenment, which cannot be measured or limited.
The World-Honored One said:

"Even if one were to combine the immeasurable fortunes of the merit of all these sentient beings and compare it to a single bodhisattva who has first resolved his mind toward enlightenment, it would fall short by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, or even a hundred-billionfold; in truth, it is empty and cannot serve as a metaphor."
"This is the foremost entry into the Samādhi of the Equal Accumulation of All Virtues for Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds.
The Buddha told Guǒsuǒ:

"Suppose all the Brahmā deities in a thousand worlds were to joyfully practice loving-kindness; and suppose there were another person who filled those same thousand worlds with the seven treasures and used them for giving as an act of charity—compared to the Brahmā deities practicing loving-kindness in those thousand worlds, the merit of that person's practice of loving-kindness would be far more excellent."
Whether it be a trichiliocosm, or up to five thousand or ten thousand worlds, or even up to a hundred thousand worlds, if one were to practice universal loving-kindness as the Brahmā gods do;

or if one were to fill a hundred thousand worlds with the seven treasures and give them away in charity—the merit and blessings planted by such an act are compared to the Brahmā gods practicing loving-kindness across a hundred thousand worlds, yet the merit of practicing loving-kindness is immeasurably greater.

Even if all beings in the three thousandfold great thousandfold world system possessed merit equal to that of a hundred thousand worlds of Brahmā practicing loving-kindness—practicing a mind of compassion directed universally toward all living beings—even calculating their merit, it would not approach, nor can it be compared by analogy, to even a hundredth, a thousandth, a ten-thousandth, a hundred-millionth, or a trillionth part of the venerable blessing of loving-kindness belonging to one who has first resolved to attain enlightenment. It is empty and beyond comparison.
Why is this? Because the virtue of one who has first resolved their will toward unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment is beyond limit.
For this reason, you should maintain this view and maintain this knowledge.
If one is able to give rise to the mind of the Great Way, then one will be fully endowed with all virtues.

If sons of noble family or daughters of noble family wish to attain the complete fulfillment of immeasurable blessings, they should give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment.
The Buddha said:
"Malla, this is the second entrance into the meditative concentration that gathers all virtues."
The Buddha said to Saṃgharakṣita:
"Regarding the worlds covered by the void of the eastern direction, can the distance of that void be measured?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
It is infinite, immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless.
O God among Gods!”
The Buddha said:
"By what analogy can the wise understand this?

The space that covers the worlds of the ten directions is inexhaustible and limitless; yet the merit, the power of concentration, the blessings, and the virtues gathered from all these qualities are even more immeasurable and far more fully perfected than that."
For the sake of sentient beings, he protects their minds with all manner of virtues and the Way, and fulfills his practices through great diligence.

Suppose there were a person who, within this trichiliocosm—from the bottom of the water's edge up to the Heaven of the Thirty-three—filled it with mustard seeds; and taking each single mustard seed as one Buddha-land, he traveled eastward, placing one seed in each successive Buddha-field until every mustard seed was exhausted. Even so, he could not reach the end of the worlds in the eastern direction.

Suppose that worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were filled with mustard seeds, and someone were to take all those mustard seeds and crush each one until they were reduced to fragments as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
“Ghoṣila, what do you think?
Is there anyone who could calculate, enumerate, or discern the number of mustard seeds that have been broken into pieces?
Ghoṣila replied:
“O Heaven among Heavens!

To break a single mustard seed into its constituent parts—were one’s wisdom equal to that of Śāriputra and to fill the entire land of Jambudvīpa under heaven, and were one to count and calculate them for the duration of an eon, one could not measure the number of those mustard seeds;
how much less could one wish to know the number of mustard seeds produced by breaking worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges?”

"Suppose there were a person who, having passed through as many Buddha-fields as there are mustard seeds, placed a single mustard seed [in each]; in this manner, they continued until all the mustard seeds were exhausted without remainder."

The world in the eastern direction is inexhaustible and its limits cannot be reached; the same is true for the southern, western, and northern directions, as well as the southeast, southwest, northwest, northeast, the zenith, and the nadir.
"It is like this, O Ghoṣila!

Suppose all the empty space within the worlds of the ten directions were filled with the Buddha-lands made of the seven treasures, and one were to give them all away as an act of charity; would not the merit obtained thereby be great?"
The Hook-Chain addressed the Buddha:
"Very much, very much,
O God among Gods!"
"It is immeasurable.
The World-Honored One said:

"The merit of a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment and practices loving-kindness exceeds the blessing of one who fills infinite worlds in the eastern direction with the seven treasures by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, and even a hundred-billionfold; it is so vast that calculation cannot reach it and no analogy can be found, just as no one is able to measure the limits of empty space."

The compassion of a bodhisattva is like space, covering everything without exception; such is the boundless reach of the great compassion practiced by a bodhisattva, as vast as the number of world-systems and buddha-fields throughout which sentient beings take form and establish their bodies.

The Bodhisattva practices loving-kindness so that all these sentient beings may achieve the status of universal monarchs (cakravartin), endowed with merits equal in number to those of Śakra and Brahmā upon ascending their thrones.

Furthermore, it is reckoned that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva establishes a pure nature, upright and free from guile, desiring to deliver sentient beings. Abiding in great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he constantly practices loving-kindness and pity. The seven steps he takes encompass merits that surpass all common folk; they are the auspicious blessings of Śakra, Brahmā, and the Cakravartin Kings. Even a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, or a trillionfold comparison cannot reach them; they are empty and beyond all metaphor.
"This is called the third entrance into the meditative state that equally gathers all virtues.
The Buddha told Guṅgula:

"If all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to possess the majestic power and merit of a wheel-turning monarch, or the auspicious merit of Śakra or Brahmā, it would not compare to the compassion of a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment."

Even if all sentient beings throughout the ten directions were to become Śakras, Brahmās, or Universal Monarchs (Cakravartins), their merit would not equal even a hundred-thousand-millionth part of a Bodhisattva’s practice of great loving-kindness and compassion.

Furthermore, suppose all the beings within the trichiliocosm were each to possess the same merit as that of a lay follower (*upāsaka*); compared to the brilliance of Śāriputra’s merit and wisdom, their combined merit would not approach even a hundredth, a thousandth, a ten-thousandth, a hundred-millionth, or even a hundred-billionth part.

Even if the three thousandfold great thousand-world system were filled with beings whose wisdom and merit equaled that of Śāriputra without any difference, when compared to the wisdom and merit of a pratyekabuddha, it would fall short by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, or even a trillionfold; it is so vast as to be empty, beyond calculation, and impossible to illustrate by analogy.

Even if all sentient beings dwelling throughout the three thousandfold world system were to become fully endowed with the virtues of a pratyekabuddha, their wisdom and merit being equal and without distinction, they would not equal—by a factor of a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, or even a trillion times—the merit of a bodhisattva who has practiced for five kalpas; when calculated, it is empty and beyond comparison.
"This is the fourth entrance into the meditative concentration that equally gathers all virtues.
When this sutra was spoken, twenty-two thousand people all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
The trichiliocosm shook in six ways;
a great radiance shone universally throughout hundreds of thousands of myriads of worlds;

the musical instruments of the devas resounded spontaneously without being struck, and celestial flowers rained down, covering the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and scattering over the Buddha until they reached his knees, pervading the entire assembly.
Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, the nāgas, and the spirits all sang praises, saying:
"Truly so, World-Honored One!

If sons and daughters of good family conceive the aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment with utmost sincerity, as has been explained by the Great Sage just now, we shall receive and uphold their teachings."

If one does not give rise to the mind of the Great Way, one will ultimately fail to attain the meditative absorption of the "concentrated intention that gathers all virtues"; how much less could one possibly achieve all the immeasurable merits and blessings!
At that time, the bodhisattva Vigatarajavikrama addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
What dharmas should one practice in order to accomplish and attain the samādhi of the ‘Equal Collection of All Virtues’?”
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"There is one dharma through the cultivation of which this samādhi is attained.
What is this one?
To resolve to develop the wisdom that masters the various supernormal powers is the first dharma for attaining this samādhi.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas for cultivating and obtaining this samādhi.
What are these two?
To listen to the Dharma and inquire about it without weariness;
and to contemplate and examine its meaning as it has been heard and received—
these are the two.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas by practicing which one attains this samādhi.
What are these three? They are:
the diminishing and elimination of all evils;
Exhorting others to gather wholesome karma;
planting the roots of manifold virtues—
these are the three.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one cultivates and attains this samādhi.
What are the four? They are:
purity of the precepts;
Their vision is pure;
their mind is pure;
their wisdom is pure.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are five dharmas by which one cultivates and attains this samādhi.
What are the five?
That which is called utmost sincerity;
a firm and steadfast disposition;
and an intention that is simple and free from flattery.
Their minds are pure and established without deviation;
they always regard all sentient beings with an impartial mind—
these are the five.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas by which one cultivates and attains this samādhi.
What are the six?
To take refuge in and rely upon virtuous friends;
To stay far away from evil friends;
to abandon and relinquish worldly assemblies;
and to practice tranquil seclusion in solitary meditation.
Practicing great loving-kindness;
having compassion for sentient beings—
these are the six.
Furthermore, there are seven dharmas for cultivating and attaining this samādhi.
What are the seven? They are:
establishing tranquility and discernment;
One should contemplate only the cessation of retribution;
govern the arising of conditions while remaining detached from the objects of perception;
and clearly understand that both transgression and merit arise entirely from causal entanglement.
To bring about equality by resolving the fetters of worldly gain;
to enter into the principles of the Way through the application of the Dharma;
and to endure abuse and insults without harboring a heart of resentment.
These are the seven.
Furthermore, there are eight dharmas by which one cultivates and attains this samādhi.
What are the eight?
The body’s actions are simple and detached;
the mouth’s speech is still and silent;
the mind’s thoughts are solitary and tranquil.
One contemplates feelings and examines all phenomena;
before the roots of evil have arisen, one does not entertain thoughts that would cause them to recur;
when the roots of evil arise and flourish, one eliminates them in accordance with mindfulness.
To cause the roots of goodness that have not yet arisen to sprout and flourish through right reflection;
and to nurture, sustain, and protect the roots of goodness that are already flourishing—
these are the eight.
Furthermore, there are nine dharmas by which one cultivates and attains this samādhi.
What are the nine?
One contemplates past phenomena and knows them to be impermanent;
Regarding future phenomena, there is nothing that arises;
regarding present phenomena, there is no duality;
having entered the three periods of time, all are entirely equal.
All phenomena are like the patience regarding dharmas;
they do not cling to emptiness;
they discern the absence of mental formations.
To be free from all aspirations;
and even when born, to provide protection and refuge—
this is the ninth.
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which one cultivates and attains this samādhi.
What are the ten? They are:
liberation from selflessness;
To endure the absence of a life-principle;
to comprehend the tracks and traces of the impermanence of non-self;
and that all that is born is nothing but suffering and affliction.
Unconditioned tranquility is itself protection;
it is the departure from perversion and the deliverance of sentient beings.
"Follow the canonical teachings;
as soon as you have heard the Dharma, practice it accordingly.
The Buddha told Vigatarajas:
"These are the ten dharmas practiced by bodhisattvas, through which they attain the samādhi of the 'Equal Accumulation of All Virtues.
Vimalatejas addressed the Buddha, saying:
'Only when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has accumulated the infinite great virtues of merit can they hear of this samādhi! "
If one wishes to resolve upon the upright and true conduct of all virtues, one should hear this samādhi;
if one wishes to obtain and fully realize the blessings of inconceivable merit, one should hear this samādhi;
if one wishes to ensure that great reliance remains inexhaustible, one should study this samādhi.
Vimalatejas again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what means does a bodhisattva mahāsattva obtain inexhaustible merit and virtue as vast as the great ocean, such that their joy is inconceivable and their meritorious legacy never ceases?"
The Buddha told Vigatamala-tejas:
"A bodhisattva has three things by which they attain inexhaustible merit like the great ocean, such that their inconceivable blessings and karmic rewards are never exhausted."
What are the three?
First is delighting in giving;
second is upholding the prohibitive precepts.
The third is to be tireless in extensive learning.
These are the three.
O son of good family!
What is meant by a bodhisattva delighting in giving?
One should not covet wealth, nor should one use material objects as inducements for conversion and teaching.
Even if there is something one is unwilling to give, the recipient should not accept that object.
If the recipient does not relinquish what they have grasped, one should not encourage them to manage their kinsmen and retinue.
If the beggar has something to request but gives rise to a mind of non-reception, one must not encourage them toward the king's wealth, treasures, productive enterprises, or houses and dwellings.
Even if a beggar should have something to request, his mind remains unchanged.
Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should give rise to this thought:
"For the sake of all sentient beings, I bestow my very life.

If anyone comes seeking anything—whether elephants, horses, chariots, clothing, or my head, eyes, marrow, brain, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, limbs, hands, feet, skin, hair, flesh, or blood—I shall give each of them whatever they seek. I shall give with a mind free from resentment, practicing patience;
having given, I do not expect a reward, and in whatever I relinquish, I harbor no craving or longing, but provide for sentient beings."
Sentient beings shall receive this grace and have their deficiencies supplied.

From this point forward, regarding all those he wishes to gather as his followers, when he attains the Way of the Buddha, he will preach the Dharma for them so that they may quickly attain understanding.
"Furthermore, noble son! If a bodhisattva resolves his mind in this way, it is said that the bodhisattva does not begrudge his body or life.

Not begrudging his body or life means that even if he were to lose his physical form, he would not commit any evil; he does not harm living beings to nourish his own body, nor does he commit unwholesome acts for the sake of his life. He does not ruin others for the sake of wealth or occupation, nor does he cause strife, litigation, or quarrels through the abundance of his kin. He does not endanger the children of others to raise his own wife and offspring. What he himself does not find pleasing, he does not inflict upon others. Having attained contentment, he gives rise to a single-minded resolve; his will finds no delight in any unwholesome matters, much less would he commit various transgressions."
Eliminating greed and envy and discarding all evils, one always knows contentment and practices what is correct and true; being without divergent thoughts, one attains equanimity.
Having attained equanimity, being free from all perversities, one obtains a mind of loving-kindness.
Having cultivated a mind of loving-kindness, one then encounters virtuous friends.
Having obtained a virtuous friend, one then hears the dharma of tranquility;
having heard the dharma of tranquility, one establishes practice;
having established practice, one transforms sentient beings.
Having transformed sentient beings, one then expounds and establishes the meaning of tranquility (*śānti*).
If a bodhisattva does not act for the sake of sentient beings and does not cultivate tranquility, then they are not sublime;
being unsublime, they do not attain the eye of the Way (*mārga-cakṣus*).
Without the Eye of the Path, one does not attain skillful means and cannot perceive the fundamental inclinations of all sentient beings.
Noble son! A bodhisattva who delights in practicing generosity attains wide renown, which exceeds even this and is beyond measure.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Contemplate the mindfulness of internal and external phenomena as one and equal; examine the internal elements and survey the external elements, seeing that they are without duality."

Why is this so? This body is like grass, wood, tiles, or stones; it is without essence, without a person, without conceptual thought, and lacks solidity, being merely a composite of the four great elements.

Even if someone were to cut, sever, destroy, strike, seize, or carry me away, I would not give rise to thoughts of resentment, nor would I harbor attachment to my body or cherish my life; I would feel no malice toward that person, but instead increase my compassion and pity for that sentient being.
For example, son of good family!

There is a great medicinal tree; one may dig up its roots, stem, joints, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits. Yet the tree does not think, "Who is taking my roots, stem, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits? nor does it think, "Do not take my roots, stem, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits."
As for that medicinal tree, it is entirely without thought or conceptualization, nor does it harbor any resentment toward anyone; when those who are ill take its medicine, they are healed.
Thus it is, noble son!
A practitioner of the bodhisattva path should regard their own body—the four great elements—as a dwelling, like a medicinal tree.
Should there be any sentient beings who desire my body, head, eyes, limbs, joints, branches, trunk, hands, feet, marrow, brain, blood, or flesh, they may take them as they please.
In this way, son of good family! The merit of a bodhisattva’s giving is inexhaustible.

Having performed such giving, they encourage and assist those who are stingy and greedy so that they may practice generosity; they transform those who are impoverished by manifesting great wealth to them; they transform those with little merit so that they may become endowed with virtue; they cause those who have not yet resolved upon the Way to practice as bodhisattvas; and they exhort them toward the roots of goodness, desiring to make them pure.
Exhorting and transforming all sentient beings through every form of auspicious merit, he guides them with purity.
By means of this giving, one quickly approaches the Way and attains the inexhaustible.
"What is meant by the exhaustion of giving?"
There are four things that exhaust the bodhisattva’s giving.
What are these four?
Not being fond of encouraging and assisting others;
One does not delight in preaching the Dharma;
one wishes to be born in a lowly place;
and one takes pleasure in associating with evil friends.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four practices by which a bodhisattva’s giving quickly approaches the Path.
What are these four?
Exhorting and assisting many;
practicing skillful means;
and establishing them in the Dharma.
Associating with virtuous friends;
these are the four.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas by which a bodhisattva’s giving is not in vain.
What are these three? They are:
generating the bodhicitta with great compassion;
and gathering and protecting all classes of sentient beings.
To reverently practice and carry out the Tathāgata’s instructions—
this is the third.
These are the three dharmas that a bodhisattva who wishes to practice giving should establish.
What are the three?
Abiding in the Buddha-dharma;
establishing diligent exposition to exhort sentient beings; and...
Thus, great peace is preserved;
this is the third.
Furthermore, there are two things by which a bodhisattva practices giving that is sincere, authentic, and free from falsehood.
What are the two?
Great loving-kindness;
great compassion.
These are the two.
Furthermore, there are two matters by which a bodhisattva’s giving is productive of results.
What are these two?
Avarice and envy; these are the two.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas by which a bodhisattva’s giving has a destination.
What are the two?
They are the perfection of wisdom; and...
The noble penetration is all-pervasive;
this is the second.
Furthermore, there are two further dharmas by which a bodhisattva’s giving has a specific destination.
What are the two?
Reaching the wisdom of inexhaustibility;
proceeding toward the wisdom of non-arising.
These are the two.
"There are four dharmas regarding the giving of a bodhisattva.
What are the four?
Giving and so forth, while not even conceiving of a reward;
being disciplined, concentrated, and tranquil;
and the perfection of what is bestowed.
Desiring to accomplish that path—
these are the four.
For this reason, whatever a bodhisattva bestows naturally leads them toward the inexhaustible ocean of virtue.
"If there are bodhisattvas who wish to be fully endowed with the ocean of virtues, they should practice such a form of giving and the conduct of diligence.
The Malla Virajatejas addressed the World-Honored One, saying,
"It is unprecedented!
O God among Gods!
Just as the Tathāgata now analyzes and expounds the dharmas of all bodhisattvas, which are sustained and protected by the sūtras of all Buddhas,
so too shall a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices in this manner never lose or destroy the virtue of correct penetration and wisdom.
"If there were someone who practiced giving in this manner, their merit and blessings would be fully perfected and complete, just like this.
The Buddha said,
"It is so, son of good family!"
It is exactly as you have said.

If one resolves to practice giving in this manner, one will then attain the inexhaustible ocean of merit; one will not be impoverished, and regarding the deeds of the sages and worthies, one will acquire great wealth.
Those of such a kind, being fully endowed with the wealth of the Dharma, attain great prosperity.

Possessing the boundless virtue of the seven treasures, they achieve the marks of a hundred blessings to adorn their bodies, serving as fields of merit and celebration for all living beings to provide for them.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Vigatarajas:
"What is meant by the prohibitions of the bodhisattva’s virtue of precepts?

It is to guard the prohibitive precepts without ever transgressing or abandoning them; to give rise to compassion upon seeing those who violate the precepts; and to see those who uphold [the precepts]..."
The practitioner should follow these precepts with firm resolve: purifying the body through three [precepts], guarding the mouth through four, and purifying the mind through three.
One should duly practice these ten wholesome deeds and, by means of this dharma of the precepts, transform others.
One should not praise oneself nor disparage others; one should not boast of one's own observance of the precepts, nor [use them] for... the sake of [self-aggrandizement].
Free from self-conceit, they constantly discipline and stabilize themselves through the prohibitions and precepts; they do not abandon their boundaries and know contentment.
Abiding in the state of the noble ones, they protect their own minds; seeing those who are indolent or negligent, they do not look for their faults.
They labor to assist the sick and emaciated without weariness, never seeking anything in return, nor regarding it as a final goal; their conduct is thus.
What is called "non-infringement" means that regarding all matters of birth and death in one's conduct, one is without partiality or aversion and eliminates all seeking and expectation;

one always stays close to the Buddha and follows a mind of compassion. Whether there are those who practice compassion or those who do not, one universally protects them with equanimity without losing this mind;
one does not deviate from the categories of precepts and does not set one's intent upon other vehicles.
Exhorting others with this vehicle of the Way, there is no peace that does not involve serving Heaven. One remains far removed from all violations of precepts and prohibitions;

those who are restless and uneasy, one exhorts and consoles so as to bring them peace; one cures and eliminates doubt so that they harbor no resentment. Wherever one is born, one attains mastery without partiality; wherever one travels, there is nothing lacking. Even if one is born [into various states], one does not grow weary; one cultivates diligence, gathers the mind, and self-restrains. One’s conduct is not disordered; in training, one has nothing to crave and nothing to fear.

"Yes, son of good family! Regarding the karmic activity of the precept category practiced by a bodhisattva: even if it should endanger their body or life, they never violate the precepts; they do not protect the prohibitions for the sake of a kingdom.

They do not do so to become Śakra or Brahmā, nor for the sake of wealth, profit, or the verification of karmic retribution; nor for the sake of retinues, noble status, handsome appearance, praise, or reputation. Furthermore, they do not protect the prohibitions for the sake of power, bedding, seats, or medicine for illness."

He does not rely on the greed born of heaven, nor does he depend on the internal or external; he does not long for others, nor does he hope for future lives; he is not attached to himself, nor is he attached to others. Furthermore, he does not crave form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor does he rely on the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind. Moreover, he does not maintain the precepts by relying on the aggregates, elements, or sense bases;
he does not fear hell to seek protection, nor does he dread the animal realm, nor fear the hungry ghosts, nor act out of concern for spirits or deities.
He does not maintain the precepts because of human poverty or distress; his resolve is solely set upon establishing the Buddha-way.

If those who hear the Dharma intend to practice it, they have already emulated the virtues of the noble assembly; they constantly desire to deliver themselves and others from the afflictions of birth, old age, death, sorrow, illness, vexation, and suffering, and thus guard the prohibitions and precepts—not for the sake of wealth or worldly affairs, but to guard the prohibitions and precepts.

They desire to bring peace to sentient beings, to shelter the multitude of sprouts, to deliver the masses, and to liberate the various classes; they delight in the Buddha-dharma, seek excellence, and aspire to turn the wheel of Dharma and nurture the assembly of sages. They do not sever the Buddhist teachings, do not neglect the instructions of the Dharma, and do not harbor worldly opinions, as they protect the prohibitive precepts.
One guards the prohibitive precepts for the sake of the categories of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
one should seek them for the sake of the six supernormal powers of penetration.

As for the precepts one follows—unviolated, unimpaired, and undestroyed, free from wrong actions, in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching without loss—one should practice the samādhi of impartial compliance.
Praised by the wise and extolled by the Buddhas, they do not deviate from the truth;

taking the transformation through the Dharma as their essential practice, such persons fully observe the constant categories of precepts and remain complete in all matters of the ten dharmas of a bodhisattva.
What are the ten [qualities] by which one shall subsequently attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin-rāja) without ever erring in the cultivation of the Sage King’s teachings?
They are: to propagate the Buddha-way without negligence;
and to preside over the station of Śakra without seeking to displace him.
They constantly receive the Buddha-way without negligence;

they ascend to birth in the Brahma-heaven without guile or eccentricity; while in the Brahma-heaven, they aspire to see the Buddha without deviation; they always encounter the World-Honored One with hearts full of joy; the scriptures they hear are never interrupted;
what they hear and receive of the Buddha-dharma is never forgotten midway; and they are able to practice and uphold exactly as they have heard it.
They maintain mindfulness of the wisdom of the assembly of noble Bodhisattvas without any loss;
their eloquence is immeasurable and never exhausted;
they attain that which was the original vow of the Bodhisattvas, and for the deeds they have established, there is a corresponding fruition.
They are never disparaged by the Buddhas or by those who are true sons of the Buddha;
their disciples swiftly attain supernatural powers and are endowed with all forms of keen wisdom;
they protect the precepts and prohibitions—one who can act in this way practices the ten dharmas of a bodhisattva.

"The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who does not regress or turn back protects this chapter on the precepts; he is guarded and protected by devas, nāgas, and spirits, who sing praises of those who maintain the prohibitive precepts.
All hosts of ghosts and spirits submit to and serve him; gods and nāgas all revere him, and the people of the world likewise offer him obedience and support."

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, always desire to behold them; all those of wisdom revere and look up to them; out of compassion for the world they practice a heart of loving-kindness, and for the sake of sentient beings they protect these prohibitive precepts.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva does not take refuge in the four destinies.
What are these four?
He does not take refuge in that which is based on a state of lack of leisure;
Nor do they return to lands where there is no Buddha;
they are not born with wrong views in households shrouded in darkness;
nor do they follow after or return to any of the evil destinies.
If a bodhisattva guards the category of ethical discipline, they shall attain these virtues.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that are never forgotten.
What are the four?
Not forgetting the Buddha-way;
not abandoning the Buddha in mind;
never interrupting the Dharma as it was heard midway through its practice.
Without losing his meditative concentration, he maintains mindfulness throughout countless and immeasurable eons.
If a bodhisattva protects these categories of precepts, he shall attain such merit.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains radiant vision.
What are the four?
At that very moment, one attains the contemplation of the luminous Dharma;
one achieves human clarity and is freed from the fears of poisonous blades and disease.
All thoughts of darkness are completely dispelled;
no one is able to disturb his various virtues—
this is the fourth.
"If a bodhisattva is able to protect the precepts and accord with this teaching, they will transcend and cross over ten fears.
What are these ten? They are:
being far removed from the fears of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, poverty, ill repute, worlds, and Māra; "
The nirvana toward which śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas aspire;

the fragile births among devas and humans that they undergo; and all manner of fears and difficulties, including those involving venomous creatures, weapons, staves, fire, snakes, vipers, lions, tigers, and wolves.
Transcending wrong views, one is able to protect the category of precepts.
Such is the practice of a bodhisattva; this constitutes the tenth effort for overcoming these difficulties.
Furthermore, son of good family!
The precepts establish the Buddha-dharma as their illumination, and the Buddha-dharma is established upon the precepts.
As for the path of the Bodhisattva, if one can uphold the precepts, one will draw near to the object of meditative concentration;
from these prohibitive precepts, one attains the practice of wisdom and liberation, and the realization of the transcendental knowledge and vision.
What is meant by the precepts that enable one to forever escape all defilements?
What is meant by "defilements" being linked to both sin and merit?
Attachment to the three realms constitutes these defilements; by what means should one cross over these various defilements?

Without thought, without ideation, without reflection, and without dwelling; without any activity, without anything established, and without any deliberation; seeking nothing among all dharmas—this is called transcending all worldly afflictions.
If, son of good family!
a bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet distanced himself from worldly defilements, he is then said to lack the category of pure precepts. Why is this so?

Even if one were to go as far as the Brahma Heaven, it would still be a realm of sensual desire; even if one were to ascend as high as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, it would likewise be a realm of sensual desire.
For this reason, son of good family!
"One should form this observation: those who dwell within the three realms possess no pure precepts.
Vimalatejas addressed the Buddha, saying, "If dwelling in the three realms constitutes affliction, why does the World-Honored One say that it is to be non-conformable with the pure precepts?"
"How does a bodhisattva become free from the dust of desire and attain pure precepts, dwelling within the triple world without being defiled?
The World-Honored One replied, "Noble son!
What is meant by "knowing"?

For one who is a bodhisattva, there are no afflictions of the body, nor is there any violation of the precepts, nor is there any fixed abiding. Yet, because they see that the multitude of beings are attached to the three realms, they thus perceive what constitutes a transgression of the precepts.

This bodhisattva practices the dharma of skillful means for two reasons: because he wishes to eliminate the three defilements, he dwells within the triple world through skillful means; though the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva himself is free from afflictions, he manifests within the triple world in order to enlighten and transform the various classes of sentient beings.
“Vimalatejas, suppose there were a man who drew figures or wrote characters in the sky; would it not be difficult for all those to appear?
He replied:
“It is most difficult,
O God among Gods!
the Buddha said.
“The undertaking of a bodhisattva is even more difficult than that; being free from afflictions themselves, they manifest within the triple world to transform and enlighten sentient beings.
Then, Vigata-mala-tejas uttered this eulogy:
“O God among Gods!...”
The Bodhisattvas, having brought forth [their vows] and perfected the infinite, practice great compassion.
Having manifested the gates of liberation, they turn back and enter again; within all their cities and strongholds, they instruct sentient beings regarding the net of obstructions.
For example, when a person develops a disease in their body, it is they themselves who must treat and eliminate the harm;
it is not another person who does so, for there is no difference between them.
Thus it is, World-Honored One!
Today one departs from harm; by means of the purity of this present life, one attains liberation through the path of the bodhisattva.
For this reason, he exhorts and transforms sentient beings as well as those of other schools; through these skillful means, he rescues and delivers all beings.
O Heaven among Heavens!
When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas give rise to the mind of great compassion, it is something that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot attain.
Why is this so? Because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas lack great compassion, skillful means,
and the practice of fulfillment.
The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Collection of All Virtues, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Malla Vimalatejas, saying: "Noble son! If a bodhisattva hears of such a course of practice, they should diligently follow it. How so?
They should seek to hear and receive instruction from their elders, always practicing respect and abandoning arrogance;

their speech should be gentle and their disposition benevolent and disciplined. They should contemplate the Dharma as being like medicine; they should regard their teacher and preceptor as the World-Honored One; they should examine themselves and contemplate the selection of the medicine of the Dharma, conceiving the thought of themselves as a King of Physicians; and they should regard all sentient beings as being afflicted by disease."

If one is intent on seeking the Dharma, one should not cherish the body, nor covet life, nor rely upon longevity; one should not long for physical appearance or clothing, but always delight in the scriptures, taking the Dharma as the foundation.
One should give away all that one possesses without stinginess, setting one's will on the benefit of the Dharma’s principles while casting aside worldly profit.

One should protect the treasure of the Dharma and remain detached from what the world prizes. For the sake of benefiting the Dharma, one eliminates all worldly wealth; by the benefit of the Dharma-treasure, one discards the precious things craved by the vulgar. Desiring to remove the stains of the afflictions and sensual desires of sentient beings, one should always aspire to seek the scriptures of the True Dharma.

If you wish to deliver all classes of sentient beings so that they all reach nirvana, you must protect and uphold them by guiding them with the True Dharma; for one who can guide and protect the scriptures of the True Dharma will be able to universally obtain the nourishment and sustenance of all roots of virtue in their practice.
For this reason, if anyone wishes to seek the Buddha-way, or desires to attain supreme perfect enlightenment, or wishes to establish the pillar of Dharma, they should study extensively.
For example, son of good family!

Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, serves as a great pillar for the heavens, like a pillar of the celestial realms; it is towering and provides vast shelter, magnificently adorning the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven wherever it stands.
The Buddha said:

"In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is extensively learned and widely informed, he becomes a pillar of wisdom; wherever he dwells, whether in the heavens or the world, his radiance and splendor are magnificent."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If there is a bodhisattva who aspires to the Buddha-way, vowing, 'I shall become a Buddha,' they must understand skillful means and extensive learning, constantly practicing with diligence. When all sentient beings abide in false wisdom, they shall kindle the lamp of wisdom for them."
If a bodhisattva, upon entering into extensive learning, diligently seeks wisdom, they will be fully endowed with the knowledge of sentient beings and have accomplished what was to be done.
At that time, the devas will raise their voices in praise and joy for such a person, and a virtuous mind will arise in them, saying:

"Now this true being, through such a character and the power of extensive learning, has attained the ten powers; having reached supreme perfect enlightenment with clear mastery of the faculties, he thus practices the conduct of a bodhisattva for the sake of such benefit and purpose."

Grasping the sword of wisdom, one cuts through all the desires of worldly afflictions; if a bodhisattva possesses such a principle as this, they will be capable of receiving the sūtras and dharmas taught by clear wisdom, and will thus be able to eliminate the afflictions and perils of sentient beings.

If there is a bodhisattva who possesses such a principle as this, they will be able to preach the Dharma to eliminate craving and desire; such a bodhisattva will then be able to take refuge in and frequent the abodes where the World-Honored Ones of the past dwelt; by means of such a principle as this, they will be able to subdue Māra and his retinue; and they will be capable of turning the Wheel of Dharma through the twelve aspects.
"O son of good family!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is diligent, widely learned, and established in noble realization, all the Māras throughout the entire trichiliocosm will immediately become sorrowful, dejected, and distressed at that very moment, thinking:
'Now this Bodhisattva does not follow my instructions and opposes my original intent; he has cast us all aside so that we no longer possess autonomy.'"
Why is this so? Noble son! Wisdom is obtained through hearing;
wisdom is the most supreme among the afflictions (*kleśa*). Since Māra cannot find an opportunity against one who is free from worldly desire, for this reason you should form this contemplation.

If a bodhisattva enters into extensive learning, discerns the sutras, and delights in the Dharma, then from that point onward, whatever they may teach will subdue and control the various māras: the māra of defilements, the māra of the aggregates, the māra of death and rebirth, and the celestial māra along with his retinue; thus these four māras will naturally be subdued.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Just as the bodhisattvas of antiquity entered into extensive learning, analyzed the principles of the Dharma, and took delight in the sūtras, I shall now briefly set forth and explain their essentials."
Furthermore, in the distant past, incalculable and limitless eons ago—vast, immeasurable, and inconceivable—a certain seer named Udraka lived during that kalpa.

Dwelling among the trees, he had attained the five supernormal powers and constantly practiced equanimity, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and protective care. While roaming and residing in secluded thickets, he thought to himself:
"As I practice a mind of loving-kindness, my body becomes supple, and I am always joyful, peaceful, and secure."

One cannot eliminate the self-willed desires of sentient beings through loving-kindness (*maitrī*), nor can one remove hatred and delusion; the vast, remote path of the desires of worldly toil cannot be traversed by means of this loving-kindness, nor can it lead to the right view of the sages and worthies.
"If one cannot bring about blessings, how could one possibly achieve the equanimous contemplation of the sages and saints?
He further thought to himself:
"One can always rely on two matters to bring about the right view of the sages and saints."
"What are these two? They are:
listening to and examining the sounds of others as a causal condition, and contemplating with a tranquil mind while remaining dedicated to practice.
Immediately thereafter, he was filled with joy and exerted great diligence, and likewise entered into the Dharma.
Thinking, "Where can I hear this teaching?
he sought the scriptures for the sake of the Dharma; yet, as he entered various provinces, kingdoms, districts, towns, villages, and hamlets seeking the sūtras, he was never able to hear them.
Then a celestial being from the realm of Māra went to where he was and said: "Noble son!

I possess a Buddha named Jāngulī, whom you should recite. If you, noble son, were to subject your body to hardship by exposing yourself to the sun every day until you hear the protective voice of that Buddha within your own body, only then would you be able to write down these verses."
"Thus, you have enabled me, O Benevolent One, to hear these four lines of this sublime verse.
At that time, O son of noble family!
the seer Uttara thought to himself:

"Since countless, limitless kalpas past, I have cast aside this body, taking pleasure in prisons, being beaten with clubs and whips, or having my body cut into pieces with sharp knives until my limbs were scattered and my flesh severed. For the sake of craving and desire, I have been subjected to bondage and encountered such innumerable calamities that they cannot be fully recounted;
yet I never valued this body, nor did I care for its perils, pains, or itching, nor have I ever used it to bring benefit to any being."
"If I am able to guide and benefit all living beings, I shall seek out the scriptures with this body that lacks solidity;
having attained such excellent benefit, my heart shall be filled with joy, and I shall receive and hear the scriptures from among gods and humans."

With a sense of the unprecedented, he gave rise to a mind directed toward the World-Honored One and maintained a spirit of reverence; he then took a sharp blade and cut his own body, exposing it to the midday sun to listen through his ears.
He then addressed the deva, saying:

"I pray that the deva will proclaim the names of the Buddhas to protect and preserve this recitation. Out of reverence for the Dharma, I relinquish my body and do not begrudge my life; by these causes and conditions, may all that has been heard be gathered together."
"At that time, O son of noble family!
Beholding the supreme seer so reverent, delighting in the Dharma, and so majestic, yet with a complexion so dark and haggard, his merit difficult to behold as he was about to vanish and disappear."
Thereupon, the High Immortal thought to himself:
"Is this not a test of my hearing this verse?
Shall I, out of reverence and in order to follow the Dharma, sacrifice my own body and disregard my life in order to hear it?"

Regarding the collection of sūtras that I have reverently compiled, may the roots of merit I have planted not lose their efficacy nor be subject to deception or delusion. If my person is truly sincere and not false, upright and without flattery, and if I have compassion for sentient beings, renouncing attachment to body and life by surrendering my physical existence, then by this truth—should there be those who hear this Dharma and practice it in this present world or in Buddha-lands of other directions—may the countenances of such people appear before me, so that I may see them and hear the teachings of the sūtra.
Having established this vow, he further spoke these words:

"At that very moment, thirty-two Buddha-lands below this world, there is a world named Samantāsamaprabhāsaviśuddhi. There, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Vimalakīrtirāja currently dwells and expounds the Dharma."
At that time, the Buddha perceived the thoughts in the mind of the supreme seer and, wishing to teach and transform the people of Jambudvīpa,

vanished from his own buddha-field in the mere twinkling of an eye— just as a valiant warrior might extend or contract his arm— and suddenly appeared before the seer, accompanied by five hundred bodhisattvas.

When that Tathāgata appeared in this world, a natural great radiance shone everywhere; hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial flowers were gathered, musical instruments resounded without being struck, and the assembly of bodhisattvas gathered in those groves.
At that time, from all the roots, stumps, trunks, joints, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of the trees upon the cliff, the sound of the Dharma issued forth.
Upon hearing of that Buddha and beholding his physical form, the supreme rishi was free from fear; immediately, his body was restored to its former state, without any scars or sores.
"Then, noble son!

The Supreme Immortal beheld the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vimalakīrtirāja, whose marks and signs were as majestic as Mount Sumeru, whose divine power and radiance surpassed the sun and moon, who was a holy and sagely sage, honored as the sovereign of devas and humans; his faculties were tranquil and settled like space, neither increasing nor decreasing, and he leaped for joy as his virtuous mind was fully manifested."
He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha:
"I am your World-Honored One; you are the Great Sage abiding in peace. I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha. May the World-Honored One, for my sake, preach the Dharma."

"If those who hear this sutra establish it and practice it in accordance with its teachings, they shall eliminate the greed and attachments of sentient beings, give rise to right view, and preach the scriptures.
"At that time, O son of good family!"

That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vimalakīrtirāja, for the sake of the rishi, expounded in detail this samādhi of the collection of all virtues for the sake of the devaputras and the bodhisattvas.
Within that assembly, eight thousand devaputras who had cultivated their conduct and refined their principles in former lives immediately attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
Upon hearing of this samādhi, the supreme rishis leaped for joy with great delight; they entered into its subtle wonder and immediately attained inexhaustible eloquence (*ananta-pratibhāna*).
At that time, that Tathāgata further expounded and summarized eight verses:
"What are these eight?
All phenomena are fundamentally pure; from the cessation of conceptual attachment, they return to their original state of natural purity."
All dharmas are without outflows, for all outflows have been exhausted;
all dharmas are without attachment, for they have transcended all objects of attachment;
all dharmas are not false, for they lack the notion of a self or a person, being equal to all dharma-gates.
All phenomena are the gateway through which all gateways of phenomena are universally manifested;
all phenomena neither come nor go;
all phenomena embrace that which comes, for they sever all destinations.
All phenomena are equal, for they neither come nor go nor abide in the three periods of time;
thus there is no duality.
This is the supreme excellence!
"The eight chapters and phrases explain that all who are enlightened and delivered grow weary of all that exists, being free from manifold afflictions.
The Buddha told the eminent and supreme seer:
"There are eight gateways of phrases that lead to non-duality."
What are the eight?
All dharmas are provisional designations, for they rely upon names;
all dharmas are like forms, for they arise from names.
All phenomena converge because they rely upon and adhere to words;
all phenomena are cognized by themselves because of their spontaneity;
all phenomena are natural because ignorance is itself natural.
All phenomena are subject to exhaustion because of practicing out of ignorance;
all phenomena have no fixed location because those who stand at the gateway abide in impermanence;
all phenomena are equal because one approaches the gateway through single-minded diligence.
"This is the supreme excellence!
It is the gateway of the eight phrases, wherein there is fundamentally no duality, yet one brings about duality.
The Buddha said to Upatiṣya:
"Furthermore, there are eight phrases of diligence that lead to inexhaustibility and the attainment of mastery.
What are the eight?
'Non-existence' refers to practicing the deeds of diligence, providing encouragement and making aspirational prayers, and manifesting the absence of a fixed locus for the sutras one practices."
That person practices the stage of diligence and is thus able to manifest the ultimate meaning of the Dharma;
"not" refers to following the stage of diligence to eliminate name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and to manifest the Dharma, causing all spoken sūtras and teachings to be completely cleared away;
"other" refers to honoring diligence to manifest the dharma of tranquility.
Sixth, to be intent upon diligent practice in expounding the sutras and dharmas, so as to transcend all obstacles;
"rootlessness" refers to contemplating the phrases of diligence to manifest the Tathāgata’s dharma of rootlessness;
"causes" refers to diligence manifesting all conditional dharmas so that both transgressions and merits may be exhausted.
"Equal" refers to the manifestation of the various destinies of all phenomena through diligence and samādhi;
this is the supreme excellence!
It is the inexhaustible eloquence of the eight phrases of diligence.
The Buddha told Shangsheng:
"Furthermore, there are eight dharmas that constitute the phrases of the sublime Dharma; to awaken to and understand all dharmas is to have an equal aspiration.
What are these eight?
The seal of emptiness is that which manifests the Dharma without any dependence;
the seal of signlessness is that which manifests the sūtras without any establishment;
the seal of wishlessness is that which manifests the Dharma without relying, depending, clinging, or seeking.
The seal-phrase of the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is the phrase of primordial emptiness; it governs all equally to manifest the sūtras.
The seal-phrase of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) governs all phenomena equally as its fundamental manifestation.
The seal-phrase of the absence of origin manifests entry into all phenomena.
It is like the seal-phrase that eliminates the fundamental manifestations of the past, future, and present dharmas;
it is the seal-phrase of cessation, which brings about ultimate extinction and forever removes the fundamental manifestations of all dharmas—
this is the supreme excellence!
These are the eight seal-terms (*mudrā-pada*); by thoroughly discerning all phenomena as equal, one attains accomplishment. Therefore, O Supreme One!
Regarding these terms of mastery, the terms of inquiry, the terms of diligence, and the various seal-terms, you should always practice them with composure and diligence in your study.
"In this way, son of good family!

Regarding the questions posed by that King Vimalakīrti, he dispatched his wisdom to that world, and together with five hundred trillion other bodhisattvas, they returned to their own buddha-field in the mere instant it takes to form a thought."
"Although he has returned to his native land, there is neither going nor coming; the people of that land do not perceive the Tathāgata as having gone or as having come.
In this regard, son of good family!"
