The supreme and victorious seer has attained inexhaustible eloquence; his mind is free from doubt or delusion and possesses no loss. He is protected by all the devas, rescuing and safeguarding the devas, subduing all Māras and external heterodox paths.
He travels through provinces, kingdoms, districts, towns, regions, and great nations, preaching the Dharma for all people, analyzing and expounding this Samādhi of the Collection of Equal Merits.

For a full thousand years, he proclaimed and manifested this scripture, transforming and enlightening eighty-four thousand classes of sentient beings so that they dwelt in the stage of Śrāvaka; inspiring eighty-four thousand beings to set their minds upon Pratyekabuddhahood; causing eighty-four thousand commoners to all resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; encouraging eighty-four thousand people so that they would all later become Cakravartin Wheel-Turning Kings; establishing eighty-four thousand as Śakra, Brahmā, and those protected by compassion, kindness, and joy; and enabling countless people to be reborn in the heavens.

From the time of the supreme seer until the final disappearance of that seer, he was reborn in the land of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vimalakīrtirāja, in the world-system called Universal Equality and Stainless (Samatā-vimala), together with fourteen thousand devaputras.
The Buddha said, "Noble son!
Do you wish to know whether that eminent and superior seer of that time was someone else?"
Do not form such a view. Why is this?
Because it was I myself.
Because I established my heart’s vow with utmost sincerity, the Tathāgata Vimalakīrtirāja has arrived from his world in the lower direction.
For this reason, son of good family!
One should contemplate in this way: for a Bodhisattva who delights in the Dharma, the Tathāgata has never entered parinirvāṇa, nor has the teaching of the True Dharma ever come to an end.
To such a Bodhisattva who takes delight in the Dharma, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of other worlds, appear before one's very eyes.

If the Bodhisattva Dharmaratī dwells in a mountain cave, or under a tree in solitary seclusion, or sits in the midst [of the forest], he immediately attains the vision of the gateways of dhāraṇī, which are placed in the palm of his hand, or appear upon his chest, or upon his head, or upon the crown of his head—near at hand and not far away.
The Bodhisattva Raticandra has already beheld the Buddhas of the past; furthermore, the devas and humans have inspired his eloquence, and he has likewise received the wisdom of eloquence from them.
The Bodhisattva Delighting in the Dharma (Ratnākara) shall never exhaust this sutra; neither the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, nor the devas and humans shall thwart his vow.
Having established himself upon the Way, he attains mastery such that he may abide for a hundred years, a thousand years, one kalpa, or beyond a kalpa, all according to his own will.

The Bodhisattva Delighting in the Dharma gives rise to his resolve by removing old age, sickness, and death; his intention is firm, enduring, and steadfast, as he is guided by the wisdom of great knowledge and eloquence.
The Bodhisattva Raticara has never, since first resolving his mind [on enlightenment], committed an offense against another. For this reason, Vigatamala!

One who hears of these practices accumulated through extensive learning and follows them with diligent application shall immediately attain such fame and virtue; moreover, they shall exceed this by many countless times.

If there are bodhisattvas who wish to attain and realize a treasury of blessings and universal virtue, whose celebration shall never end and whose emolument shall be inexhaustible; the merit and fortune of such bodhisattvas are so vast that they are immeasurable, beyond all calculation, and their limits cannot be reached.
Vimalatejas! One may know how to count every drop of water in the great ocean and measure its limits to find the mud at its bottom;
yet the three things undertaken by a bodhisattva—precepts, learning, and the bestowing of gifts—cannot be surpassed or limited, nor can their boundaries be reached.

The three thousandfold great thousandfold world system may still be weighed to know its exact grain-measure and its very limits; yet, as for exhausting the three matters undertaken by a bodhisattva—precepts, learning, and generosity—their path is immeasurable.
This, noble son, is the Chapter on the Practice of the Three Matters.
Among these three matters, extensive learning is the most honored, the most excellent, the most preeminent, and without equal.
It is like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains;
keeping the precepts and practicing generosity are like mustard seeds at the side of Mount Sumeru—one should regard extensive learning as being like Mount Sumeru itself.
For example, when a bird soars through the void, how could its shadow cast upon the ground possibly equal the vastness of space?
Such is the nature of observing the precepts and practicing generosity.
Just as space is vast, universal, and boundless, so too is the virtue of extensive learning.
Why is this so? O son of good family!
Giving has two benefits: it brings freedom from poverty and destitution, and it results in the attainment of great wealth.
Precepts have two benefits: they deliver one from the evil realms and cause rebirth in the heavens.
Hearing has two benefits: it acquires noble wisdom and removes false doubts.
As for giving, it does not transcend the aggregates (skandhas) that are subject to outflows (āsrava).
Those who uphold the precepts still possess the aggregates (skandhas) they have received along with the outflows (āsravas).
Those who are widely learned, however, are free from all outflows and do not receive the aggregates.
For this reason, Vigatarajas!
"This is what is called the Bodhisattva’s appropriate response to extensive learning.

When the Buddha spoke on generosity, morality, and extensive learning, thirty-two thousand beings planted the roots of manifold virtues and all resolved to attain unsurpassed, true, and perfect enlightenment; five hundred bhikṣus, their outflows exhausted and minds liberated, attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Thereupon, the Mārapramardaka Vīra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"By practicing how many dharmas does a bodhisattva swiftly attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas?
The Buddha said:
“O son of good family!
There are four practices of the bodhisattva by which one swiftly attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
What are the four?
First, one attains liberation by contemplating the body as being like a shadow;
second, one enters into all phenomena as being like the resonance of an echo;
and third, one clearly understands that the mind is like a magical illusion.
To observe that all phenomena ultimately return to extinction—
this is the fourth [quality] by which a bodhisattva quickly attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, there are four other qualities.
What are the four?
Universally cultivating great compassion and extending it to all sentient beings;
even if a student conceives the notion of a person, encouraging them to achieve understanding so that they may know all dharmas are ultimately non-existent and not subject to conditioned activity.
To universally behold the Dharma of all Buddhas— not by means of the fleshly eye, nor the divine eye, nor the Dharma-eye, yet without anything upon which to rely;
to clearly and thoroughly understand that which the mind enters, wherein there is neither mind, nor perception of mind,
nor any causal conjunction— this is the fourth.
Furthermore, there are four.
What are the four?
To give all that one possesses without being stingy;
Abandoning false views;
upholding pure precepts;
and pacifying and eliminating worldly afflictions.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are another four.
What are these four?
Abiding in the power of patience, they enter into all dharmas;
they thoroughly know and exhaustively investigate them,
while revering and exalting diligence.
Delighting in the dharma of detachment;
these are the four.
Furthermore, there are another four.
What are the four?
Attaining meditative concentration without any dependence;
examining wisdom without frivolity or playfulness;
To embrace skillful means without attachment to sentient beings;
and to fully possess all practices so as to enter the peerless state—
these are the four.
Furthermore, there are four.
What are the four?
Constantly practicing great compassion to guide and benefit sentient beings;
Being fully endowed with great compassion, they do not weary of the beginning or the end;
practicing great joy, they delight in the Dharma;
practicing great protection, they eliminate all attachments.
These are the four.
There are another four.
What are these four?
It is proven to be partially contained within the three gates of liberation;
it eliminates the distinctions of the three periods of time—past, future, and present;
and it transcends the triple world.
"Contemplate that all phenomena are fundamentally pure and without defilement.
The Buddha said,
"Vimalatejas!"
"These are the four practices by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva swiftly attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, the Bodhisattva Vigatarajas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas; filled with joy and leaping for gladness, he ascended into the air to a height of forty-nine chi above the ground.

The trichiliocosm shook in six ways; a great radiance shone universally throughout the world as celestial flowers rained down, and hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts of the Bodhisattva Vimalatejas, immediately smiled with joy; five-colored light issued from his mouth, illuminating countless Buddha-lands in the ten directions, then circled him three times and re-entered through the crown of his head.

The worthy Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha with a verse of praise, saying:
“Having attained noble and pure wisdom, Your eyes are clear and bright;
All your faculties are tranquil and settled— This is the perfection of serenity.”
His radiance shines for seven feet; his golden countenance is majestic and sublime.
For what reason do you manifest this joyful smile?
I only pray that you will explain it for me.
He knows the conduct of all devas and humans, and where their minds are directed;
he perceives the purity of the three periods of time through their various manifestations.
His wisdom is ever-penetrating, never encountering any obstruction.
For what reason do you manifest this joyful smile?
O Moon-like One, please speak out of compassion.
You were a God among Gods in past ages, and you shall be the World-Honored One in future ages.
The Buddhas currently manifesting throughout the ten directions possess wisdom that flows boundlessly;
their practices are entirely pure and white, and they heal manifold ailments, leaving nothing unclarified.
We pray that you will explain this for us in detail.
His body pervades everywhere throughout these Buddha-lands;
his speech is fully expressed across countless realms.
His heart is directed toward all people, constantly bestowing vast and great compassion.
Supreme One, out of compassion, please explain for us the meaning of this smile.
You have thoroughly mastered the Dharma wherever you go; you are as serene as the moon’s journey through the sky.
It is beyond analogy, like a magical illusion; it is spontaneous, like a dream.
The gains and benefits you have attained are as transient as bubbles rising from rain;
for what reason do you manifest such joyful laughter?
You who are a lion among lions without a teacher, you who understand emptiness and are free from conceptualization, you have transcended the gates of vows and liberation.
All phenomena are of their own nature; you have fully realized the ultimate meaning.
Silent and ever-tranquil in meditative concentration, you move through the world like space.
I pray that the Buddha will distinguish the intent of his mind: what has moved you to smile now, and how may it be healed?
Who has given rise to the wondrous mind, vowing for the supreme awakening wisdom?
Who shall empower the removal of Māra, so that one may sit beneath the King of Trees?
Who today is the most excellent, providing transcendent protection?
For what reason do you manifest this joyful smile?
O Great Hero, please explain it.
The assembly of śrāvakas is unable to tread upon this ground.
None of the pratyekabuddhas dare to reach this path;
it is the realm of all Buddhas, whose virtue is like the great ocean.
By what cause do you smile with joy?
“The World-Honored One speaks of him with compassion.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Did you see Liǎojùwēi (Vimalatejas) leaping into the air, four zhang and nine chi above the ground?”
He replied, “I have seen them,
O God among Gods!”
The Buddha said:

"The Bodhisattva Vigataraja-vikrama, after passing through incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and true awakening as a Most Rightly Awakened One. He shall be known by the name Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. He will dwell in an eastern world named Viśuddha, during an eon named Praśastaviśuddha."

The pure world of the Tathāgata Balavyūhaśuddharāja is prosperous and flourishing; its people are peaceful and secure, grain is cheap and abundant, and its happiness is unsurpassed, with countless devas and humans dwelling therein.
The clothing, food and drink, dwellings, and houses of the people in that land are like those in the fourth heaven, Tuṣita.
That Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma contains no extraordinary or diverse teachings; he merely proclaims the treasury of the bodhisattvas.

In that buddha-land, there are no names for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; it consists entirely of bodhisattvas who have attained the patient endurance of dharmas (dharmakṣānti), and the assembly of bodhisattvas is vast and limitless.

The lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable; his land is free from the calamities of the eight difficulties; he has subdued all demons and suppressed all enemies; and there are no swarms of heretics or followers of external paths.
The ground of that Buddha-world is of deep blue lapis lazuli, with purple-golden sand interspersed throughout.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vimalatejas descended from the void, prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, took refuge in the World-Honored One, and requested permission from the Buddha to leave the household life.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śṛṅkhalā approached the Buddha and addressed him, saying: "Yes!
O God among Gods!"
How truly marvelous and unprecedented!
Now that the Great Sage expounds the sutras, there are various devas in the void whose names and virtues are sublime; they all approach the Tathāgata.

As soon as they behold the Tathāgata, they are filled with joy, cast off their thoughts of arrogance and self-importance, and prostrate before the World-Honored One, surrendering themselves in refuge.

The Great Sage is indeed able to transform and enlighten this Vimalatejas Māraputra, who was arrogant and conceited; having come to the Buddha’s presence and attained the Great Dharma, he shall now expound the sutras and teachings for the sake of immeasurable and inconceivable classes of sentient beings, so that they may eliminate their pride and indulgence.
"Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
From how many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas did the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vigataraja plant the roots of all virtues, that he was able so swiftly to attain such supernormal powers?"
The World-Honored One said: “Ghoṣila!

If you wish to know this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vigataraja-vikrāmin, he has already made offerings to sixty-two billion Buddhas, the Great Sages; he has planted the roots of all virtues and established himself in the unsurpassed, right, and true path. He shall again serve countless Buddhas and purely cultivate the Brahma-faring.”
The Hook-Lock (Gongsuo) asked again:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
By what root of non-virtue planted did he forget his aspiration for the Way, harboring a mind of arrogance and self-importance, and come before the World-Honored One wishing to test you?"
The Buddha told Saṃgharakṣita:
"There are four things that cause a bodhisattva to forget the aspiration for enlightenment while practicing the bodhisattva path.
What are these four?"
The mind harbors arrogance;
one does not revere the Dharma;
and one treats virtuous teachers with contempt.
To slander and criticize from behind;
these are the four.
Furthermore, there are another four dharmas.
What are the four? They are:
repeatedly taking pleasure in associating with the assembly of śrāvakas and sharing the same refuge with them;
and being inclined toward and delighting in inferior deliverance.
Slandering bodhisattvas;
forgetting the kindness of the Dharma teacher— these are the four.
Furthermore, there are four.
What are the four?
Their conduct is characterized by flattery and deceit.
Arrogance and insolence regarding the Dharma;
sustaining oneself through two [unrighteous] means;
and seeking gain and offerings while being attached to servitude.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are another four.
What are these four?
They do not perceive the works of Māra;
they are shrouded by their transgressions;
and they are entangled and obscured from the Dharma.
Having a timid and weak disposition,
and being bound by fetters—
O Kausika! These are the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva forgets the aspiration for the Way.
Gongsuo, listen further!
For what reason did Li-gou-wei abandon the aspiration for the Way while practicing as a bodhisattva?
In ages past, during the beginning of this Bhadrakalpa, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Krakucchanda Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Mahāśāla-Sudhana, of noble lineage and immense wealth.

He had a son who, deluded by Māra, became arrogant and refused to go to the presence of the Tathāgata to receive the Dharma that brings long-term benefit. Together with other śramaṇas, brahmins, and elders, he engaged in quarreling and abuse, slandering many; he was unwilling to accept the Dharma, did not perceive the Dharma, failed to find a teacher of the Dharma, and neither honored nor followed his instructions.
In this present life, one will incur five losses.
What are these five? They are:
being separated from the Buddha so as no longer to see him; and not being able to hear the Dharma.
They no longer establish the deeds of a bodhisattva nor inquire about them;
they forget the roots of all virtues that ought to be practiced;
and they lack a firm resolve regarding the mind of enlightenment.
"When one grasps at unwholesome thoughts, one then departs from the mind that practices the Path.
At that time, thought departs from these five modes of practice.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Kauśika! Do you wish to know who was known at that time as the son of the brahmin Mahāśāla of the noble Śāṇakavāsin clan?
Could he possibly have been anyone else?"
Do not hold such a view.
Why is this? It is because he is none other than the present Bodhisattva Vigataraja-Tejas!

At that time in that world, although he harbored conceit and soon forgot the intent of the path he had cultivated, he later again protected the roots of virtue from his past lives and the mind of various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
Furthermore, because he possessed residual merit and did not again slander those supernormal knowledges, he became a strongman of great power.

Receiving the Buddha’s sacred command, they shall refrain from all evil deeds; upon hearing the Buddha’s voice, they shall come forth spontaneously, desiring to match the Tathāgata by their own power.

Furthermore, hearing the World-Honored One speak of the power of Bodhisattvas, they will immediately cast aside arrogance, pride, and self-indulgence. Through the roots of various virtues planted in the past, they will then manifest before them and attain the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), possessing majestic supernormal powers and wisdom free from all conceptualization.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śaṅkalābandhana addressed Vimalavikrama:
"O son of noble family!
By giving rise to what dharma does one attain the patient acceptance of dharmas (dharmakṣānti)?"
Vimalatejas replied,
“It gives rise to all the dharmas of ordinary beings.
He asked again:
“How is it generated? He replied:
“That which is generated reaches ultimate exhaustion such that it is forever non-existent, yet it is not something other.”
"What he initiates never again allows for any dependence, nor is there anything to be realized.
Gouluo asked again: "Noble son!"
"What difference is there between the dharmas of ordinary beings and the dharmas of the Buddhas?
Could there be any distinction at all? He then replied:
"Names are established through provisional designations; though there may be various [terms], their underlying meaning is no different.
He asked again:
"Indeed, son of good family!..."
Regarding the dharmas of ordinary persons, by what principle are they explained? He replied:
“They are impermanent and devoid of conceptualization; this is the principle of being free from inversion.”
He asked again:
"Noble son! As for what is called 'meaning' (artha), where does it ultimately lead?"
He replied: "Gongsuo!
One who has attained the true meaning neither eliminates the dharmas of ordinary beings, nor does he acquire the dharmas of the Buddha-way."
He asked again:
"Noble son! What is meant by 'the meaning of the Dharma'?"
He replied:
"There is no duality of meaning; it is the meaning of all dharmas.
He asked again:
"It is not said:
'One who possesses right view has two causes and conditions—hearing it from another or reflecting upon it—and yet their practice remains complete.
Gouluo asked again:

"The Tathāgata does not say that one attains the essential meaning merely by returning to it; rather, the meaning itself constitutes the essence. For what reason, then, would one seek the essence through the meaning instead of grasping the elegant phrasing?"
He replied:
"If one does not merely grasp at the essential meaning but never destroys it, is that not the elegant expression for a bodhisattva?
In that case, there is no fault; rather, it is self-destruction."
Even if there were one who attained excellence in words and meanings, that which he had reached would likewise be nothing gained.
Such a bodhisattva does not rely on essential meanings when teaching the meaning of the Dharma, owing to his wisdom and sagacity.
Without attaining anything further and without requiting it through righteous means, he possesses sovereign mastery over all dharmas; he is the honored one, the elder, and the peerless.

That which can be conceptually differentiated is extinguished within its limited time, reaching ultimate nirvana; when both the beginning and the end are eternally quiescent, this constitutes the meaning of "mark" (*lakṣaṇa*).
For this reason, O Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One has spoken thus: it is like a chain!

As for the meaning of taking refuge, it is not to grasp at dharmas; there is neither recollection nor one who grasps, neither relinquishing nor grasping. That which is without recollection is the firm and essential; that which is firm and essential is what is called "meaning."
Gongsuo (Hook-and-Chain) asked again:
"Venerable son of noble family!
Is there a method or calculation by which one returns to the essential meaning, such that one then returns to the essence of all dharmas?"
He replied:
"There is, son of good family!
He asked again:
"For what reason? He replied: "All dharmas have no fundamental basis;
all are entirely empty and all dharmas are tranquil. If one returns to the essential meaning of emptiness, the essential meaning of tranquility is likewise so. For this reason, son of good family!"
The essential meaning of its ultimate destination is that the Way returns to all dharmas.
He replied: “Noble son!
The Buddha did not say:
"To fully comprehend all dharmas, they must all return to the essential governance. He replied:

"It is so! For this reason, when one investigates the fundamental meaning and origin of all phenomena, that which is their essential destination and ultimate meaning—this gateway is the primary meaning."
How should one seek that which is as it is?
One who seeks in this manner practices such a way that there is neither dharma nor non-dharma, neither arising nor ceasing.
The various noble paths of the sages are not two paths; they involve neither action nor non-action, neither non-doing nor the absence of creation. To be thus is to create the path of a bodhisattva.
"The Way is without fabrication and does not seek meaning; its ritual forms are never confused.
When Vigour Free from Defilement (Vimalavikrama) spoke these words, five hundred bhikṣus and eight hundred devaputras were distanced from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
The Bodhisattva Vigatarajavikrama addressed Saṃdhinirmocana, saying: "Noble son!
That which the Tathāgata has spoken returns solely to the essential meaning; he does not take up elegant phrasing."
When one calculates this meaning, there are no two modes of practice; even when one reaches its ultimate meaning, there is nothing that arises. Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of this meaning alone!
One should simply return to the essential meaning and not grasp at elegant phrasing.
As for the essential meaning and the elegant phrasing, they are fundamentally pure and equal; the nature of the will is spontaneous and beyond transcendence.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has said:
"One should take refuge in the essential meaning and not grasp at elegant phrasing."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
For what reason does the Tathāgata speak these words? It is because of two matters that right view arises.
What are these two?"
Listening to the voices of others and reflecting upon them through contemplation:
those who have not extensively heard the Dharma and Vinaya follow their samādhi from beginning to end while falling into arrogance; such is the reason for this.
The World-Honored One said:
"To listen to and examine the laws and teachings is to possess broad learning and receive much encouragement and assistance.
By listening to the sutras and the Dharma and practicing them all accordingly, one purifies that which is to be treated, reaching the path of the sages and saints.
He asked again:
“What is meant by a bhikṣu’s practice of contemplative treatment?
He replied:
"To practice the healing through the Dharma while practicing nothing at all—this is the essential matter of contemplation that constitutes the healing practice.
Son of good family!
This is what is meant by 'the healing practice.'"
Furthermore, son of good family!

Suppose a bodhisattva practices healing without uttering sounds or giving rise to the notion of a self, yet speaks concerning the various spheres of practice—whether speaking of going or speaking of returning—in all these cases there is neither abiding nor anything to be attained; there is neither the past nor the future, nor does one cultivate these matters in the present. This is called practicing healing by means of essential contemplation.

If one perceives that all phenomena are naturally and entirely subject to extinction, and if one receives and contemplates the essential purity of all phenomena, even if one examines and sees that all phenomena are fundamentally pure and identical in form, one likewise beholds their essential purity.
If one perceives all phenomena as arising naturally from primordial purity, one should also contemplate essential purity.
If one perceives that all phenomena are fundamentally and ultimately unarisen, being ultimately without origination and ultimately without cessation, one should also contemplate essential purity.

If one contemplates that all dharmas are fundamentally pure and in a state of extinction (nirvāṇa), and yet contemplates essential purity, neither remaining in quiescence nor having anything to observe—this is called contemplation.

That which is observed is itself without observation and without seeing; if there is neither seeing nor observing, then even such a "seen" is not seen, and thus it cannot be called having something seen.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Vimalatejas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!"
Regarding that which is spoken, it should be as you, O Benevolent One, have spoken.
For one who intends to purify their essential thought as a bodhisattva, the Dharma is not false or deceptive.
For one who intends to purify their essential thought as a bodhisattva, the Dharma is free from the hindrances of the aggregates.
For one whose contemplation is essentially pure and who acts as a bodhisattva, there is neither this dharma nor any gate of liberation.

For one whose contemplation is essentially pure and who acts as a bodhisattva, regarding the dharmas they practice, there is nothing to be eliminated, nothing to be practiced, and no coming or going; this is the equal contemplation that constitutes right view.
"Because all dharmas are seen as equal, they are not unequal, just as they are seen.
He asked again:
"In what way are all dharmas not unequal, such that they are seen as having been seen or as not having been seen?"
"Furthermore, son of good family!
These dharmas neither have a joyful perception nor a non-perception; they are equal from beginning to end and are without arising—this is what is meant!"
Neither is there anything produced, nor is there anything that exists; it does not transcend what is seen, nor does it enter into quiescence—this is called equality.
It is neither non-existent, nor is there anything that exists; it is neither spontaneous, nor is it non-spontaneous—this is called equality.

That which is spoken is likewise without anything being said; its practice is without arising, and it is without view or transcendence. It is equanimous and quiescent; this is called "equal contemplation," for it is able to enter into equanimity.
Again, he asked once more:
"For what reason is it called 'equally entering into tranquility'?
He replied:
"Equal to the self, yet also not the self; all dharmas are likewise without form and without disparagement—this is called entering equanimity into tranquility."
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Saṃdhāna addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
It is truly unprecedented that one enters correctly into quiescence; the characteristics by which this occurs are fundamentally pure and extinguished. Bodhisattvas know all such dharmas in this way.”
"If there are those who hear this and are able to believe and understand it, even as they dwell and travel about, they shall not attain parinirvāṇa midway.
The Buddha told Guǒsuǒ:

"For this reason, a bodhisattva takes joy in skillful means (upāya-kauśalya); through these skillful means, they cultivate and fulfill their practices, giving rise to all minds and returning to the four dharmas of dwelling and traveling."
What are the four?
Practicing great loving-kindness;
possessing boundless compassion;
To attain all supernormal knowledges;
and not to sever the Buddha's teachings—
these are the four.

If one is able to respectfully propagate and cultivate this Dharma, one will enter the state of quiescence toward which all things tend; all things are fundamentally pure and entirely extinguished, reaching the practice of the various dharmas that are utterly still. Having heard this, one then believes and delights in it, and though one may dwell and travel therein, one does not attain parinirvāṇa midway.
Therefore, when one discerns the source of all phenomena, that [source] is quiescent; it is neither stagnant nor does it fall away.
Why is this? Because one does not wish to abandon any sentient being.
The Bodhisattva Vigataraja addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way is a bodhisattva pure and virtuous, such that, as the Buddha has said, they do not fall into cessation?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Noble son! If a bodhisattva is without any views and without conceptualization, this is what is called being pure and wholesome.

Yet, toward all śrāvakas and all sentient beings, they do not cultivate equanimity, they depart from the teachings of the Buddha-dharma, and they neither encourage nor delight in the practice of the Mahāyāna.”

Doubting that the various supernormal wisdoms are apart from wishlessness, yet not entering nirvāṇa into quiescence, one thereby realizes the bodhisattva mind therein; though one's intent lies with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one enters into nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, son of good family!
If a bodhisattva can enter into the state of quiescent characteristics, they will be able to discern all dharmas; whatever they initiate will be entirely for the sake of all beings.

They accord with the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; they follow and cultivate the Mahāyāna; they abide in the arising of all supernormal knowledges and wisdoms; they take pity on all classes of sentient beings; they universally perceive all things in accordance with their aspirations; and they never cease to provide for the needs of others.
"For this reason, son of good family!
You should form this view: consider that bodhisattvas are all pure and virtuous, dwelling in tranquility.
Vimalatejas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is unprecedented,
World-Honored One!
The conduct of Bodhisattvas possesses such extraordinary distinction that it is entirely beyond the reach of the stages of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.”
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Saṃdhāraṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“This Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta here in this assembly sits in profound stillness; he does not even expound this samādhi.”
The World-Honored One, perceiving the thoughts in Mañjuśrī’s mind, mentally invited Puṣya (Prabhūtaratna) the Youthful.
Puṣya the Youthful then addressed Saṃdhinirmocana Bodhisattva:

“Regarding the conduct of a bodhisattva, one pursues the Buddha-way not for the sake of merit, nor for gain and offerings, nor for rebirth in heaven, nor for wealth and enterprise, nor for fame and renown; rather, one does so to praise virtue and proclaim one’s achievements.”
"It is not for the sake of clothing or food, bedding or rest, medical treatment for illness or emaciation, nor for the occupations of livelihood, nor because of rewards granted by kings or ministers.
Gūṣa again asked the Bodhisattva Prabhūtaratna:
"For what reason do you practice the path of a bodhisattva?"
Puṣya replied: "For the sake of sentient beings, out of compassion for them, I employ the principles of the Dharma to transform and enlighten the masses;
and because my aspiration lies in the Mahāyāna, I eliminate the afflictions of all vain and weary labors."
Because birth is quiescent, one has already endured toil and suffering;

desiring to bring peace to sentient beings so that they may attain their aspirations, and because one is free from doubt and free from longing, one is then without attachment and without reliance, without anything received, without dwelling exclusively in any place, and ultimately there is no "excellent" (sādhu) to be found!

Furthermore, he does not conceive of a self, nor does he harbor such thoughts; he neither regresses nor turns back. If all dharmas are immovable, he is neither agitated nor trembling, neither departing nor arriving; he is neither harmed nor elated, neither sorrowful nor dejected. He alone is courageous and valiant—unconquerable, unsubduable, unsurpassable, and never withered.

Free from fear or difficulty, neither terrified nor apprehensive, neither abrupt nor violent, and without arrogance; furthermore, with no discursive mind, always dwelling in tranquility, constantly abiding in non-conceptualization, sharing the same purpose as the One Vehicle, and through the single teaching and identical manifestation always performing equal practices—all this is for the sake of wishing to rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
Viśeṣamati said: "Noble son!
The conduct of a bodhisattva is of such a nature; it is for this reason that they undertake their practice."
The Hook-and-Chain again asked Pūrṇamukha:
"What is it that one practices and constructs to constitute the conduct of a bodhisattva?
Pūrṇamukha replied:
“Furthermore, son of good family!

When a bodhisattva does not practice within exhaustion, neither arising nor non-arising, having reached the ultimate end of all exhaustion and that which is to be exhausted; when they do not dwell on the beginning or the end, nor on non-arising or non-production; and when they are without cleverness or contrived action—this is the practice of a bodhisattva, and it accords with the practice of the Way.”
Furthermore, O Ghoṣila!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not practice with a mind that exhausts the past; he does not give rise to any practice regarding a future mind; and he does not dwell upon, nor engage in any practice regarding, the present mind. Furthermore, his mind does not cling to the past, the future, or the present.
To practice in this manner constitutes the conduct of a bodhisattva; this is what accords with the path of the Way.
Furthermore, Kausika!

Regarding the mind of the Way in sentient beings, there is no duality between it and the Tathāgata. Likewise, in the case of precept-keeping, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom, there is no duality between the Way, sentient beings, and the Tathāgata.

If a bodhisattva constantly adheres to these six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and practices them, the characteristics of their practice will not cause anxiety regarding the beginning or the end; practicing in this manner constitutes the conduct of a bodhisattva, and thus accords with the path of the Way.
