"Furthermore, Kausika! That which the bodhisattva follows is not the practice of emptiness regarding form; for form is empty of itself.
Nor does he practice the emptiness of sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; for consciousness is naturally empty.
Furthermore, he does not teach others to practice the emptiness of form, for form is simply empty."
When both the root and the branches are entirely non-existent, this is called "spontaneity" (*zìrán*). Feeling, perception, volition, formation, and consciousness are likewise empty.
If one desires to exhaust [these factors], since both the root and the branches are entirely empty, it is said that consciousness is empty, which is also called spontaneity.

If that which has already been exhausted were to exhaust all dharmas, and if all dharmas were to be exhausted, then form would also be exhausted; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness would likewise be exhausted, and consciousness would thereby come to an end.
If all forms were to be exhausted, then all dharmas would likewise be exhausted;
if all dharmas were to be exhausted, consciousness would likewise be exhausted.
If a bodhisattva practices such as this in accordance with the bodhisattva path, they will then be acting in accord with the Way.
Furthermore, Śṛṅkhalābaddha Bodhisattva!
The conduct of a bodhisattva neither severs the practices of ordinary beings, nor does it zealously engage in the practice of transcending birth and death for the sake of the Buddha-dharma;

it does not fully realize the matter of extinction (nirvāṇa), nor does it perceive the arising of unwholesome dharmas, nor does it observe the origins of wholesome dharmas, because it does not rely on [discriminative] wisdom.
Nor does one perceive consciousness; it is not by means of consciousness that one perceives wisdom.
Furthermore, one does not destroy the practices of the dharma-realm, but through faith and joy, arrives at liberation.
If a bodhisattva practices in accordance with such conduct for a bodhisattva, they are then practicing the path.

Furthermore, son of good family, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva undertakes this practice, although the dharma-realm is immeasurable and the realm of sentient beings is limitless, they have full faith and understanding that the dharma-realm is limitless; thus, the realm of wisdom and the realm of sentient beings are both exhausted, and the dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings as they are practiced are non-dual.

The dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is neither diminished nor exhausted; perception is likewise so, and the realm of persons (pudgaladhātu) is also thus. While the realm of persons possesses characteristics, the dharma-realm is without characteristics; as for that which shares such characteristics with the realm of persons, it is itself without characteristics.
Being without marks, one perceives that all phenomena are entirely without marks.
One does not exhaust the realm of persons, yet acts with fearlessness; this arises and is brought forth from the thought of non-essentiality.

Deceived and deluded by inverted matters, they dwell amidst these conditions; yet in their practice, they do not eliminate the dust of desire, nor do they long for rebirth; they seek neither fame nor renown, nor do they calculate permanence; they do not undergo destruction, nor do they extinguish the notions of self, person, or life-span.
"If a bodhisattva practices and cultivates such conduct as this for the sake of the bodhisattva path, they shall accordingly proceed upon the way.
When this chapter on "The Conduct of Bodhisattvas" was being spoken, hundreds of thousands of devaputras attained the patient acceptance of dharmas (dharmanidhyānaksānti).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimalatejas immediately sought permission to speak, raised his voice in a great sound, and uttered this eulogy:

"May all classes of people and sentient beings have their wishes fulfilled and universally obtain beneficial profit, just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, causes them all to believe in and delight in this samādhi."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān said to the youth Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta,
"Am I capable of praising the bodhisattva path according to the conduct of a bodhisattva?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"It can be practiced," the Māra then said:
"The practice of all people is the practice of a Bodhisattva; [therefore, it can be practiced]."
The practices of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are the bodhisattva practice;
the practices of those dwelling in households who carry the burden of the aggregates (skandha) are the bodhisattva practice;
and all the practices of Māra are the bodhisattva practice.
"Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas shall dwell together therein, and all must learn this bodhisattva training.
Then the Bodhisattva Saṃdhāna went to where Māra was and said to him:
“How does a bodhisattva learn all things universally?
Māra replied:
“There are eighty-four thousand types of conduct among sentient beings:”

Twenty-one thousand belong to those of greedy temperament, twenty-one thousand belong to those of angry temperament, twenty-one thousand belong to those of deluded temperament, and twenty-one thousand belong to those of equal temperament; all such categories are entirely encompassed within the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Therefore, O Ghoṣila!

One may practice the conduct of desire while remaining free from desire; practice the conduct of anger while remaining free from anger; practice the conduct of delusion while remaining free from delusion; and practice the conduct of equal proportions while remaining free from equal proportions, such that one is ultimately without attachment.
Furthermore, son of good family!

If there is a bodhisattva who universally follows the conduct of all sentient beings, he will then be able to thoroughly examine the conduct of the multitudes and transform and enlighten all classes of living beings.
"If there is a bodhisattva who practices in this way as the conduct of a bodhisattva, then they should be practicing the Way.
He then asked Māra:
"What is meant by 'all the deeds of Māra being the conduct of a bodhisattva'?"
He replied:
"It is because Bodhisattvas must enter into the mental activities of all Māras.

They do not regard arising as arising, nor do they follow the instructions of Māra’s deeds. They fully comprehend the conduct of Māras and transform it into the conduct of benefiting sentient beings; they observe what those [Māras] practice, yet they do not cultivate such practices themselves."
While remaining alone among the hosts of Māra, he manifests the non-practice of demonic deeds;
furthermore, he should train in the governance and transformation of Māra, so that even while amidst the Māras, there are no demonic activities.
He asked the Māra again,
"What is meant by saying that the conduct of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas constitutes the bodhisattva practice?
The Māra replied:
“O son of noble family!

Suppose a bodhisattva, for the sake of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, expounds the Dharma so that their aspirations are fulfilled; yet, remaining within those practices, he honors and increases his own conduct of diligence and seeks this wisdom, rather than attaining parinirvāṇa by means of those vehicles.”
Furthermore, son of good family! All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) proceed spontaneously; they are the practice of profound stillness.

That which a bodhisattva should believe in and delight in practicing is a practice that has transcended all practices, a practice of ultimate truth. All conditioned phenomena have no abiding place; all conditioned phenomena are entirely unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) practices, neither joined nor assembled. They are practices that do not arise and practices that do not abide. A bodhisattva should revere such a practice.
The Māra King again asked Puṣya:
"May you deign to show us favor and once more explain these various practices?
Puṣya replied:
“With eloquence capable of accomplishing all, one transcends everything; all such spheres constitute the conduct of a bodhisattva. Why is this?

Because that practitioner does not conjoin with the eye-element, nor does he meet with the form-element; he does not conjoin with the ear, sound, nose, odor, tongue, taste, body, tangibles, mind, mental objects, or the mind-element.”
For this reason, Māra, you should form this observation: one who is able to transcend all realms is called a true gentleman (satpuruṣa).
Furthermore, O Devaputra!
If a bodhisattva can practice in this way, they do not deceive or mislead the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Such practice is the practice of a bodhisattva; it is the practice that accords with the Way.
He asked again: "What is it,
Puṣya, that constitutes the practice of a bodhisattva which does not deceive or delude the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and all dharmas?"
The Bodhisattva Puśya replied:
"That which the Tathāgata has spoken is the truth: he has realized that all phenomena are empty and entirely non-existent, and has thereby attained supreme perfect enlightenment."
If a bodhisattva relies upon the view of the body and all Buddha-dharmas, and likewise views nirvāṇa, then they deceive and delude all the Tathāgatas.
O Devaputra!
If one wishes to know the practice of the Tathāgata, it is by being without conceptual attachment toward any phenomena that one attains perfect enlightenment.
If a bodhisattva were to have conceptual seeking or dwell within conceptualization regarding any phenomena, they would be deceiving the Tathāgata.

"Son of Heaven! The Tathāgata is authentic, real, and truthful; he has no point of origin, nor does he arise, nor does he emerge. He possesses nothing, relies on nothing, and is without marks. He comes from nowhere and abides nowhere. His original nature is pure, his original nature is luminous and penetrating, and his original nature is quiescent nirvāṇa—just like empty space, which has no form or appearance."
The understanding of all phenomena is likewise entirely thus, whereby one attains perfect enlightenment.

If a bodhisattva, regarding these phenomena, perceives coming and going, entering and exiting; if that which arises appears suddenly, emerging from existence and depending upon signs; if there is coming and returning, or anything established; if there is no purity, or if there is the circling through beginning and end amidst afflictions; or if one acquires forms and possessions and becomes negligent—then whatever such thoughts one harbors constitutes a deception of the Tathāgata.
Suppose, O Devaputra!
there is a bodhisattva who, through equal mastery, understands emptiness and realizes that all phenomena are entirely free from conceptualization regarding any views;
and who, through equal mastery of conduct, understands all phenomena and completely eliminates all perceptions.
Equanimously governing all phenomena through the wishless and non-conceptualization, they transcend the triple world;
equanimously governing all phenomena as being like space, they do not cling to original purity.
A bodhisattva who practices in this manner does not deceive or mislead the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
At that time, the Great Sage praised Pṛthuśāsana, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
O Youthful One!"
"Practicing in this way constitutes the bodhisattva practice.
If a bodhisattva practices in such a manner, they will swiftly receive the prediction of enlightenment.
The Buddha said:
"Samantabhadra!

I recall that in the past, during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I exhorted myself to practice the pure dharma; though my practice was non-practice and not even extinction, I received the prediction of enlightenment."

Why is this so? Abiding in all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is called "the manifested light. Having beheld this, what need is there for conceptualization or volitional formations (*saṃjñā-saṃskāra*)?

At that time, one perceives form as it truly is and sets the mind upon the benefit of the ultimate meaning; having just received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) from the Great Sage Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, one realizes original purity. Immediately, one universally understands that all dharmas are entirely without arising. Only thereafter does one receive the prediction as seen by the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara.

In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood, known by the name Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat; at that time, you will immediately attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).
For this reason, Puṣya!

If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to swiftly attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), they should cultivate this practice to rescue those who regress. Their mind should be without attachment; they should not pursue the Dharma through the zeal of worldly gain. There is nothing to be liberated and nothing to be delivered; it is precisely by having nothing to deliver that one attains liberation.
Puśya again asked the Buddha:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
When one attains the patience regarding dharmas (dharmakṣānti), what is it that is reached?”
The World-Honored One said:

"One does not attain the patience regarding the Dharma by apprehending form; nor does one attain the patience regarding the Dharma by apprehending feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness."

One does not attain the patience of the Dharma by concealing the various sense-bases; one does not attain the patience of the Dharma by calculating permanence, emptiness, purity, tranquility, or a self-body; furthermore, one attains the patience of the Dharma by forever perceiving that no phenomena whatsoever can be apprehended.
The Buddha said:
“Puṣya! Because all dharmas are utterly exhausted, they are called ‘non-attainment.’”
"Viśeṣamati!
The patience of dharmas (dharmakṣānti) is neither attained nor obtained; it is called 'attainment' only because it conforms to worldly conventions.

It is not the dharma of ordinary beings, nor the dharma of those in training (śaikṣa), nor the dharma of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), nor the dharma of pratyekabuddhas, nor the dharma of bodhisattvas, nor is there any practice that constitutes the dharma of the Buddhas."
Because one does not engage in any activity whatsoever regarding all phenomena, it is called "attaining the patience of the Dharma through its exhaustion.
Because all phenomena are likewise unattainable, it is therefore called "attaining the patience of the Dharma through its exhaustion."

If the patience toward dharmas (dharmakṣānti) is empty and non-existent, one has no fear regarding any perceptions or any conditioned activities; therefore, it is said that by seeking them exhaustively, one attains the patience toward dharmas.

He has no eyes, nor is there eye-consciousness; he has no ears, nor is there ear-consciousness; he has no nose, nor is there nose-consciousness; he has no tongue, nor is there tongue-consciousness; he has no body, nor is there body-consciousness; he has no mind, nor is there mind-consciousness. When all fears are exhausted, this is called the patience of dharmas (dharmakṣānti).

"The unconditioned realm is called the patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*); the absence of a mental realm is called the patience regarding dharmas; when all things are completely exhausted, one attains the patience regarding dharmas.

When he spoke these words on the patience regarding dharmas and the complete exhaustion of all dharmas, five hundred bodhisattvas attained the non-arising patience (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*). In a single voice, they raised their voices and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, World-Honored One!"
We shall fully assemble the samādhi of the equal gathering of all virtues, and we shall also universally prepare for all dharmas so as to reach the state of non-arising.

This profound and subtle Dharma is that which all bodhisattvas should study, receive, and follow; if there are those who hear it, they should joyfully believe, accept, uphold, recite, and practice it according to the Dharma.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Saṃdhinirmocana said to Mañjuśrī: “It is said:
‘What was to be done has been accomplished; all tasks have been fulfilled.’”
“By how many dharmas should a bodhisattva ensure that all the deeds they undertake are brought to ultimate completion?
Viśeṣacintin replied: “Noble son!
If there is a bodhisattva who knows all dharmas yet performs no action, such a bodhisattva has completed what was to be done and has attained ultimate accomplishment.
Since all dharmas are entirely non-existent and have no sphere of activity, one who understands all dharmas in this way has completed what was to be done and has attained ultimate accomplishment.
There is neither wisdom nor duality; what was to be done has been accomplished and is ultimately perfected.
It is neither apart from action, nor is it non-action, nor is there non-non-action; what was to be done has been accomplished and is ultimately perfected.
One who possesses something has that which is proclaimed; having completed what was to be done, they achieve ultimate perfection.
One who receives grace repays the grace received; having completed what was to be done, they achieve ultimate perfection.
Having encountered those who are ungrateful, one responds with gratitude; having completed what was to be done, one achieves ultimate perfection.
Those who should offer worship do so with humility and self-effacement; having completed what was to be done, one achieves ultimate perfection.

One who understands reciprocity and one who is free from reciprocity; one who can accomplish tasks and one who is free from failing to accomplish them—having completed what was to be done, they achieve ultimate fulfillment.
One who treats others with ease and one who meets with neglect or harm—prostrating in salutation, having completed what was to be done, they achieve ultimate fulfillment.

Regarding that which is performed, one does not apprehend the practice of the dharma of what is performed; regarding that which is encountered or observed, one does not apprehend what has been traversed; having completed what was to be done, one achieves ultimate perfection.
If a donor exhorts others to enter the Path, they have accomplished what was to be done and attained ultimate fulfillment.

They neither apprehend giving nor apprehend the Path; they neither apprehend a self, nor apprehend a person, nor apprehend another. Having accomplished what was to be done, they attain ultimate fulfillment.

He does not guard the precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, or wisdom, nor does he guard anything else while exhorting others to advance toward the Way; having completed what was to be done, he has attained ultimate fulfillment.

If there are those who practice giving, observing the precepts, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom, and are encouraged to enter the Path, they will have accomplished what was to be done and attained ultimate fulfillment.
Neither wise nor foolish, without self and without other, and with nothing to be attained, one has accomplished what was to be done and reached ultimate fulfillment.

One practices various virtues through bodily actions, verbal expressions, and mental intentions; yet, when discerning these matters, even the various virtues practiced by body, speech, and mind are neither attained nor clung to. This is called having accomplished what was to be done and reaching ultimate fulfillment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Constant Firm Diligence said to Mañjuśrī:
"Should I go and declare that the deeds of a bodhisattva have been accomplished and are ultimately perfected?"
Puśya replied, “I am capable!
The son of good family said to Puśya:
"If one encourages even a single person to hear the sound of the Way, their task is accomplished.

When the Bodhisattva’s treasury is at its full capacity according to the occasion, if they cause others to attain the Buddha's voice, the Dharma's voice, and the voice of the Noble Assembly, then one should examine this: their task is accomplished."

If one transforms a single person, causing them to receive the precepts and prohibitions, to take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha, and to set their will upon the Triple Gem, then what has been done is complete.

To fully provide the treasury of the Bodhisattva’s offerings—whether it be the places where they dwell, those who give, or those who receive—and to encourage these two parties to aspire toward the Way, constitutes the pure merit of the Bodhisattva.

If there are those who give and those who receive, and one encourages and transforms them through this practice of the Dharma—these two matters are both the pure and meritorious blessings of a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva contemplates mindfulness of the Buddha, or further contemplates the Dharma, the Sangha of noble ones, other bodhisattvas, and sentient beings, their task is accomplished.

The Bodhisattva receives offerings as one who holds a precious casket. Even if a Bodhisattva practices the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, should they encounter a single person who is base, impoverished, a thief, or a butcher—one who insults them with words that burst forth from the mouth—they are able to endure it. Without succumbing to anger, they continue to practice loving-kindness and meet that person with a joyful heart. Desiring to benefit and assist them, they increase their diligence even further; thus, what was to be done has been accomplished.

Whether one obtains a hundredfold profit, a thousandfold profit, a hundred-thousandfold profit, or a hundred-thousand-ten-millionfold profit; or if one were to fill Jambudvīpa with precious jewels to obtain such profit—one has never used those jewels to incite double-tongued speech. Furthermore, when consulting others regarding wisdom, one would rather lose body and life than follow after them to speak evil.

He does not forget the Dharma and does not accept what is contrary to the Dharma; observing this, one sees that the deeds of this bodhisattva are already complete and he has attained ultimate accomplishment.
"Furthermore, Puṣya!

Suppose a bodhisattva were to abstain from offerings for seven days and fail to obtain food; yet, if there were another person who received food and drink, that person would be close to the mind of universal wisdom and would not be acting in vain.

Furthermore, desiring to deliver and liberate all sentient beings, and wishing to provide succor to the multitudes of living creatures, one should observe the ultimate accomplishment of the deeds of this Bodhisattva.
Even if the entire world were filled with water reaching its very limits, one should cross over it and proceed to seek the hearing of the Dharma;

even if it were filled with fire, one should likewise cross over it and proceed to seek the hearing of the Dharma. One should not begrudge the body, nor covet life, nor cling to longevity, yet cultivate this contemplation. The aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are easily obtained, but the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are difficult to encounter; the sutras and the Dharma are difficult to hear, and encountering those who are reverent toward the Dharma is likewise rare. If one enters into such contemplations, this Bodhisattva has attained ultimate accomplishment.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva hears a verse of four lines and leaps for joy, they would not wish to enjoy the fortune of becoming a wheel-turning sage king; rather, they would prefer to cause others to hear even a single four-line verse so that they may attain joy and gladness, rather than delighting in the rank of Śakra.
It is better to stand and use various gifts to guide and transform dogs, beasts, dragons, and spirits than to be reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
One should delight in the mind of all-encompassing supernormal wisdom and not covet the seven treasures of the trichiliocosm.
With joyful exultation, one should aspire to plant even a single root of virtue, rather than seeking the benefit of offerings from all sentient beings.
When a bodhisattva practices and cultivates in this manner, one should observe that the bodhisattva achieves ultimate perfection.
The Bodhisattva Constantly Firm in Diligence again addressed Puṣya:

"There is a bodhisattva who is constantly firm in diligence and always seeks extensive learning; he should keep this in mind: even if someone were to cut his body into pieces, limb by limb, he should give rise to joy and encourage himself, thinking, 'All of this is brought about by worldly phenomena.'"

With single-minded devotion to practice, they keep the Buddha-way in mind; they would rather lose their lives than ever violate the precepts or abandon the Mahāyāna. They do not succumb to ignorance nor give rise to the power of evil. They achieve the power of patience so that their speech is never coarse, remaining fully capable of endurance. Ultimately, they never grow indolent but cultivate the practice of diligent effort.

They purify Buddha-fields and save sentient beings without engaging in unrighteousness; they universally seek all the *pāramitās* without seeking companions or hoping for the favor of sentient beings; they firmly abide in wisdom and do not sever the Buddha-teachings; their will and nature are powerful and fierce, such that there is nothing they undertake that they do not accomplish.

His mind is benevolent and harmonious; he has cast aside greed and frivolity, harboring no longing or attachment. He does not spare his own body or life, being thoroughly skilled in what is appropriate and expedient. He causes those who have not yet established themselves to find refuge and to uphold the precepts with purity. He is the first to inquire after others' welfare, speaking with gentle words that are free from ornate embellishment; he is like the earth, detached from all seeking.

Having no desires and no attachments, their nature and conduct are purely good; their responses are peaceful and their teachings are always refreshing. They respectfully accept wholesome admonitions, cast aside arrogance, and always maintain a humble disposition. Their words are most sincere and free from anger or dispute; what they say is according to reality, without slander or flattery. Their words and deeds correspond with one another, and they honor an impartial mind. Feeling compassion for all sentient beings, they always possess a heart of loving-kindness and direct their will toward great pity for all living creatures.

For the sake of the common people, he remains without flaw; he establishes the foundation of all virtues and maintains a heart of joy. He bestows all that he possesses without begrudging it, and through his conduct, he protects and rescues those who have needs. Having acquired wealth and resources, he acts with tranquility; he relinquishes all greed and attachment, harbors no sense of "mine," and does not rely on possessions. Ultimately, he is never arrogant and eliminates the three defilements.

Resolutely seeking liberation and remaining free from conceptualization, one’s thoughts and attachments shall not fall into various views; being free from the sixty-two [wrong] views, one should practice extensive learning, be fully endowed with the seven riches, and always maintain a courageous mind. One should never grow weary of what is heard and understood, but should study wisdom so as to establish it, dwelling in valor to subdue the afflictions.

Free from the defilement of desire, he heals the illnesses of all sentient beings; ever acting as a protector for the multitude, he never abandons them. Having perfected the field of merit through the mind of universal supernormal wisdom, he causes all sentient beings to receive his grace.
Their conduct is like a lotus flower, unattached to all worldly things; they are like a ferryman who delivers all living beings across the afflictions of the four illnesses.

Their resolve is like a royal highway, such that they do not treat with contempt those of high, low, or middle station. They should be like the source of a spring, a stream, a river, or a great river, such that the sūtras they preach are inexhaustible. Their practice is like the great ocean, and the wisdom they have heard encompasses boundless depths; it is the accumulation of immeasurable virtues. Their nature is like Mount Sumeru, appearing in the world as most precipitous and lofty. They always delight in diligence, their disposition is magnanimous, and their mind is neither timid nor inferior. Their mind is like a threshold, their vows are firm, and their will is like a crane’s down.

Harmonizing their nature, they should practice the honored mind; delivering and guiding sentient beings, they cultivate mastery. Encouraging and assisting their resolve, they maintain a marvelous and elegant spirit.

Their subtle and wondrous liberation is like that of Śakra, and their gathering of sentient beings is like that of Brahmā. Discerning expedient means and pure conduct, they attain mastery over all dharmas.

One should always practice compassion to achieve ultimate *nirvāṇa*; even if one encounters offenses as if at the end of one's life, one should be able to endure them all, whether they are committed against oneself or not.

One’s mind should be like a strict father toward that which is most weighty; one’s resolve should be like that of a companion in establishing the roots of all virtues without attachment, and the will should have nothing upon which it relies.
Regarding all sensory objects, one practices without harm, cultivating loving-kindness and benevolence; wherever one is born, there shall be auspiciousness.

One becomes a donor of the Dharma, severing all unwholesome dharmas and practicing all manner of wholesome dharmas; following the path of non-negligence, one eliminates self-indulgence, arrogance, and pride.

Training in the precepts with diligent practice and firm resolve, one cultivates the bodhisattva path without negligence; only thus can one attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and become a most perfectly awakened one.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Constant Firm Diligence, saying:
"Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!"
It is truly marvelous how the Bodhisattva’s practice thus establishes all virtues.
If a bodhisattva wishes to attain the Samādhi of the Equal Accumulation of All Virtues, they must universally discern all merits and remain free from all faults and transgressions.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Saṃdhāna came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If there is a bodhisattva who attains this Samādhi of the Equal Collection of All Virtues, to what may its meritorious auspicious responses be compared?”
The Buddha told Saṃgharakṣa:

"As for this Samādhi of the Accumulation of All Virtues, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains this concentration, they will be able to remain far removed from the realms of evil destinies and will never encounter the eight types of calamities or hardships. They will eliminate poverty and destitution, becoming naturally wealthy and joyful with abundant provisions. With all their faculties complete, they shall then be able to accomplish the thirty-two marks of a Great Being."
The Dharma is inexhaustible, and he attains eloquence; having acquired dhāraṇī, he never loses his mental focus, and he exercises mastery over all merit and virtue.
He becomes a wheel-turning monarch, free from dependence or obstruction, and is venerated by all the masses.
He was praised by Śakra, Lord of Devas, and the Brahmā gods bowed their heads in prostration before him.
Having attained supernormal powers, there was nothing he did not clearly understand; he achieved his original vows and attained mastery over his place of birth.
Employing skillful means and wisdom in advancing and retreating, one does not follow the teachings of dhyāna but cultivates wisdom.
Detached from all views, this state is supremely distinguished and noble, beyond the reach of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Free from all fears, they transcend the discriminative wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; with their faculties fully awakened, they understand the origins and ends of sentient beings and bring them joy amidst various views.
Their resolve is fixed upon the matters of the single-minded gate of liberation; abiding nowhere, they always accord with what is bestowed.
Established in the precepts, they maintain the threefold purity; through their discernment of patience, they are ultimately formless and free from thoughts of flattery or hypocrisy.
They proclaim diligence with a resolve free from weariness, and explain meditative concentration as the constant transcendence of stillness.
He expounds wisdom, constantly beholding and discerning all things; his eyes are free from attachment and he ever relinquishes them, never straying from the removal of the six sense-bases.

Constantly seeing the Buddhas, he delights in hearing the Dharma; he serves the assembly of noble ones and practices with earnest diligence, never departing from emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

Regarding the sūtras and hymns he hears that praise the merits of all Buddhas, he receives them all as the Buddha’s instructions and consults upon them accordingly, skillfully analyzing and explaining them for the sake of sentient beings.
In the Tuṣita Heaven, they never abandon the dharma of non-retrogression; if they wish to travel through all buddha-fields, they do so without obstruction, universally beholding all Buddhas.
Having subdued the enmity of Māra, they are free from the four māras; seeing the profound patience of the Dharma, they abide in the stage of non-retrogression.
Attaining the clarity of supernormal powers, they remain within the path of practice, such that there is no dharma they do not master extensively.
With a mind that comes to rest in tranquility, one perceives with pure clarity; the practices performed bring the Buddha-dharma to fulfillment, manifesting non-retrogression.

As for the direction toward which these practices tend, all attachments are eliminated. Whatever obstacles there may be regarding the perception of a self or physical form, they are seen to be like illusory manifestations. Observing and seeing them all, one realizes that among all bodies, none can surpass this: namely, those followers of other paths who receive and protect the True Dharma, and those who, following the honored scriptures of the Buddhas, do not spare their own bodies or lives.

Their conduct is diligent as they uphold and govern upright righteousness; they manifest the realm of the Buddhas, which is eternally and perpetually uninterrupted; though they have entered *nirvāṇa*, they do not pass into extinction.
Attaining fearlessness, they move among assemblies without dread or difficulty.
Intelligent, wise, and far-reaching, he skillfully eliminates whatever he undertakes and casts away all arrogance and conceit.

He cultivates the Great Adornment and, through the *māyā-samādhi*, produces such a profound influence that it is as if he emits a radiance that completely eclipses the sun, moon, stars, fire, and lightning.
They attain firm and powerful strength; their bodies are like linked chains and their conduct is like adamant. They transcend all evils and deficiencies.

Universally purifying the site of enlightenment, they travel through immeasurable Buddha-lands, universally hearing their voices. Established by the Buddhas, their body, speech, and mind are pure, subduing the armies of Māra.
They attain the perfection of the supernormal power of transformation, shaking all the buddha-fields.
They acquire brilliant wisdom, discerning the ultimate destination of the meanings of the Dharma.

Possessing perfect eloquence and unimpeded wisdom, they practice diligence for the sake of all sentient beings; they manifest and exalt the Buddha-work without negligence, and within all penetrating wisdoms, they manifest the realm of the Buddhas.
Thus it is, O Ghoṣila!

If there are bodhisattvas who attain this Samādhi of the Accumulation of All Virtues, the auspicious signs, causes and conditions, manifestations, and the renown of the various virtues of these bodhisattvas shall be as magnificent as this.
The Chain-Link addressed the Buddha, saying:
“May all classes of sentient beings together attain this Samādhi of the Collection of All Virtues. Why is this? Because—”
"Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
If there are those who attain this samādhi, their manifold virtues and renown will be so magnificent that they cannot be matched by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
"If there should be anyone who hears this samādhi and does not believe it, you should know that they are certainly being tormented by Māra.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!"
"Kauśika! It is exactly as you have said.
If there should be anyone who believes in this samādhi, their merit and virtue will be inconceivable, and they shall be protected by the Buddhas."
Thereupon, Ghoṣila again asked Puṣya:
"If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to attain the Samādhi of the Equal Accumulation of All Virtues, what dharmas should they practice?"
Puṣya replied:

"If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to attain the Samādhi of the Equal Accumulation of All Virtues, they should practice this conduct without ever disparaging the dharmas of ordinary beings; yet, regarding the dharmas of the Buddha-way, they shall have no attainment whatsoever."
If one wishes to practice, one should practice this way: there is no dharma, no view, and no cause for anxiety.
Furthermore, Kausika!

If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to attain this samādhi, they should vow and exhort themselves from beginning to end that they will not be defiled by birth and death, that they will attain the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and that they will not seek parinirvāṇa through the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, Ghoṣila!

A bodhisattva who wishes to attain this samādhi and be endowed with all virtues should train in the precepts that are to be learned. Moreover, they should not form thoughts regarding outflowing merit, outflow-free virtue, or the absence of fault or non-fault; they should neither affirm existence nor non-existence, neither cling nor abandon, neither depart nor arrive, and neither transcend the world nor remain within it—never entertaining such conceptualizations.

Equally honoring the Dharma-realm and taking joy in its manifold virtues—whether merit or demerit, permanence or impermanence, mindfulness or non-mindfulness—they do not enter into the marks of attachment regarding the cycle of beginning and end.
One enters into all virtues for the sake of all people, rather than dwelling in the blessings and merits for the sake of a single person.

Because the virtue of one person universally enters the realms of all sentient beings—whether those blessings are with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—one no longer makes such distinctions, nor does one teach by means of this [dualistic] instruction.
One should form this thought: the virtues of all Buddhas are the virtues of a single Buddha.
Regarding those whom they teach and transform, one should believe and know that the preaching of the various Buddha-dharmas is without distinction or difference.

Whether it be the merit of what is learned, the merit of what is not learned, the merit of a pratyekabuddha, the merit of a bodhisattva, or the merit of a Tathāgata—these are all impermanent and devoid of form, shape, or appearance; one should joyfully believe in and delight in them as the convergence of all virtues and merits.
For example, O Ghoṣila!
Just as all forms and shapes consist of the four great elements, so it is with the dharmas of all bodhisattvas:

they all deliver sentient beings to the gate of liberation and practice equal merit; yet that which is to be done and that which is brought to flourishing is subject to the law of impermanence and exhaustion.
"Furthermore, Kausika!
If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to attain this meditative concentration, they shall harbor no fear regarding the four immeasurables.
What are these four?
The realms of sentient beings are immeasurable;
the Buddha-fields are limitless;
the Buddha’s wisdom is boundless.
The conduct of sentient beings has no fixed limit;
this is the fourth.
Furthermore, O Hook-and-Chain!
If there are bodhisattvas who wish to attain this samādhi, they should always encourage and assist in the four inconceivable things.
What are these four? The retribution of sin and merit is inconceivable; [the second is]...; [the third is]...; [the fourth is]...; the retribution of sin and merit is inconceivable.
The conduct of sentient beings is inconceivable, yet the path they follow is without distinction;
the wisdom of the bodhisattvas is inconceivable, as are their supernormal powers, spiritual strengths, and doors of liberation;
the destination to which the bodhisattvas proceed is inconceivable, and their births are pure.
These are the four. Therefore, Ghoṣila!
If there is a bodhisattva who perceives the inexhaustible within this samādhi, they should practice these four dharmas.
What are the four?
In this regard, the establishment of a bodhisattva’s merit is inexhaustible;
the fulfillment of all practices is likewise inexhaustible.
Unimpeded eloquence is also inexhaustible;
that which wisdom reaches is also inexhaustible.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four matters.
What are the four?
Diligently applying effort toward the Dharma, accumulating the roots of manifold virtues without ever becoming weary;
One should mindfully apply oneself to entering into the hearing of the sūtras without weariness and to preaching them;
one should mindfully apply oneself to exhorting and assisting in the boundless virtues of all manner of goodness;
and observing the adornments seen in all buddha-fields, one should enter one's own field to bring it to purity.
"These are the four.
The Bodhisattva Saṃdhāna said to Mañjuśrī:

"For example, when lapis lazuli, moon-pearls, and precious jewels are placed within a vessel—whether it be a vessel of gold, silver, crystal, or musaragalva—it does not lose its natural brilliance because of the majestic power of the lapis lazuli, moon-pearls, and precious jewels."
Thus it is, Puṣya!

If there is a bodhisattva who dwells in this samādhi—whether living at home or having gone forth as a śramaṇa—they reckon that the natural course of the dharma-realm is the gate of liberation of non-duality.
Furthermore, Puśya!
What practice does a bodhisattva follow and cultivate so as not to lose samādhi, and what enables them to attain inexhaustible virtue and wisdom?
Puśya replied:
“Kausika! If you wish to know what a bodhisattva should practice, there are four matters.
What are these four?
Not begrudging one's own body or life, they do not seek the benefit of any offerings;
practicing emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they do not aspire to the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;

desiring to attain the Buddha-wisdom, they contemplate its practice, and regarding all supernormal knowledges and wisdoms, they relinquish all thoughts and conceptions, whether appropriate or inappropriate.
"All sentient beings equally enter the practice of the perfections (*pāramitā*), yet the self, the person, and the life-span are likewise unattainable.
These are the four.
Ghuṣmaka again asked Puṣya:
"Where does this samādhi ultimately lead?

If a bodhisattva takes up a scripture and wears it upon their person, or gives rise to patience—whether they live as a householder or have gone forth to study—is this due to the causal practice of learning and conduct?"
Puśya replied to Saṃdhinirmocana:

"If, in the future, there should be one who attains this samādhi, even if someone merely hears its name, that person will no longer be subject to the conditions of either the household life or the life of renunciation."
Why is this? Therefore, O Ghoṣila!

If a bodhisattva dwells in samādhi, they will be free from dualistic conceptions; wherever they travel, their lifespan and wisdom shall be inexhaustible and beyond limit, with nothing forgotten or lost.
He transforms and enlightens sentient beings without ever becoming weary, yet he does not manifest himself in the form or appearance of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, regarding all that is presented, it is entirely boundless and devoid of causal conditions.
For example, O Ghoṣila!
Just as the sun and moon travel through all boundless realms, so too does the Bodhisattva contemplate non-reliant practice.

Whether dwelling in the state of a householder and relying upon household life, or not leaving the home life yet engaging in the conduct of one who has left it, he likewise does not cling to the virtues of renunciation; in these two matters, he harbors no longing.
Why is this? Because that which issues forth from a bodhisattva is entirely without attachment.
It is like, O Hook-Lock! [a chain].
One who has nothing to attain achieves perfect enlightenment; regarding this, there are four practices for a bodhisattva.
What are the four?
To be honored, to be supreme, and to be most excellent.
To cast off all objects of perception and to enter into the Dharma of all Buddhas—
these are the four.
The Hook-Chain (Aṅkuśa) again asked Pūrṇamukha:
"In what manner does a bodhisattva dwell?
Pūrṇamukha replied:
“Bodhisattvas have four practices.
What are the four?
Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.”
These are the four.
Whoever practices these four Brahma-vihāras, I call that dwelling.
Furthermore, there are another four.
What are the four?
If one dwells and resides in villages or houses while wandering, that constitutes dwelling in a place of travel.
Even if one practices while staying in a secluded retreat, or if one practices while on a loft or a multi-storied building, that likewise constitutes dwelling in a place of travel.
"These are the four.
Pu-shou (Mañjuśrī) further said to Gou-suo (Śṛṅkhalā):
"If one does not practice these four Brahma-vihāras, yet thinks to oneself, 'I dwell and roam [in this state],' that person is deceiving all devas and humans."

Why is this so? The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have taught that the four Brahma-vihāras constitute dwelling; these four Brahma-vihāras abide at the summit. This is pure conduct through which one dwells; while remaining within the realm, one receives almsfood, and its majestic spiritual power rests upon the summit.
Therefore, Ghoṣila! Those who do not perceive the four Brahma-vihāras are far removed from the practice of the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).

Furthermore, those who cultivate pure Brahma-conduct all arise from and follow the four Brahma-vihāras to attain the wisdom of the noble ones (*āryajñāna*); they do not regard themselves as superior in the world, nor do they eliminate the notion of "self" through arrogance or conceit.
Guṅs-skyes (Śaṅkha) again asked Pūrṇamukha:
"How does a bodhisattva practice the conduct of loving-kindness?
What is meant by compassion?"
"What is meant by joy?
What is meant by equanimity? Puṣya replied:
"To use illusory phenomena to rescue and protect all classes of sentient beings is the practice of loving-kindness;
to use illusory phenomena to deliver sentient beings is the practice of compassion;
and to use illusory phenomena to bring peace and security to the multitude of living beings is the practice of sympathetic joy."
To teach that one causes all sentient beings to attain nirvāṇa through illusory phenomena is to practice protection.
Furthermore, Kausika!
To have faith and understanding that the realm of sentient beings is empty is to practice loving-kindness.
To have faith and resolve that the realm of phenomena and the realm of sentient beings are neither created nor uncreated is to practice compassion;
to have faith and resolve, and to know with understanding, that the realms of all living beings are neither attached nor liberated is to practice joy;
to have faith and resolve, and to know with understanding, that the realms of the masses come from nowhere is to practice equanimity.
Furthermore, Kausika!
When all sentient beings are without a self and yet feel no fear, this is the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*);
when all sentient beings are entirely tranquil and yet feel no dread, this is the practice of compassion (*karuṇā*).
To remain without fear regarding the equality of all phenomena within the dharma-realm is the practice of joy;
to have faith, understanding, and discernment regarding all buddha-fields as inexhaustible lands is the practice of protection.
Furthermore, Ghoṣila!
That which is characterized by the absence of harm is called loving-kindness (maitrī);
that which is characterized by the absence of peer comparison is called compassion (karuṇā).
The absence of dualistic characteristics is called joy;
the absence of names and the characteristic of non-attachment is called protection.
Furthermore, O Hook-Lock!
Compassion that dwells nowhere is not Great Compassion;
pity that dwells nowhere is not Great Pity.
Why is it said that it is not Great Compassion?
It is just as when a śrāvaka gives rise to this thought:
"May all sentient beings attain peace and security.
This compassion of a śrāvaka is not the Great Compassion.
What is called great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*)?
If one maintains an impartial mind toward all classes of sentient beings and delivers them all from the afflictions of suffering, this is called great loving-kindness.
What is called compassion (*karuṇā*) that does not constitute great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)?

To feel pity and compassion for the masses of beings born within the five destinies, desiring to rescue and deliver them from the midst of birth and death—this is called compassion (*karuṇā*), but not great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
What is called great compassion?

It is to behold the common folk undergoing birth and death within the five destinies, and to exercise pity and sorrow wherever they are born; to personally relinquish one’s own bodily peace to rescue and protect those in the five destinies, thereby being able to deliver sentient beings from their realms and immediately establish them upon the path of equality—this is called great compassion.
Therefore, Ghoṣila!
You should form this view: the compassion of the śrāvakas is not the Great Compassion, nor is their pity the Great Pity.
Therefore, Ghoṣila!
"If there are bodhisattvas, they should fully practice great loving-kindness and great compassion.
When Prabhūtaratna had spoken these words, eight thousand devas and humans all resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
They all exclaimed together:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We, too, shall practice this conduct just as it was just now taught by Puṣya."
A hundred thousand devas and humans attained this samādhi, and eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Saṃdhinirmocana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Tathāgata, we pray that you will explain the marks of the hundred merits. By what meritorious deeds did the Buddha, the World-Honored One, accomplish these marks?”
At that time, the Buddha said:
"For example, O Saṃgharakṣita!

Suppose all the Buddha-worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were gathered together, and every sentient being within them were fully endowed with merit; the merit of all these beings combined would constitute the virtue of a single Universal Monarch (Cakravartin). Furthermore, if the merit possessed by all those sentient beings were each equal to that of a Holy Universal Monarch, and all such merits were combined together, they would constitute the merit of a single Śakra, Lord of Devas."

Furthermore, suppose there were other Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, and all sentient beings therein were made to fully achieve and possess merit equal to that of Śakra, Lord of the Devas; and suppose all the merit of these sentient beings were combined together, equaling the merit of Śakra—only then would it reach the merit of a single Brahmā-deva.

Furthermore, suppose there were sentient beings in as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and each of them possessed merit equal to that of Brahmā; if the merit of all these sentient beings—each equal to that of Brahmā—were combined, it would constitute the merit of a single śrāvaka.

Furthermore, suppose there were other Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and within them, each class of sentient beings possessed merits equal to those of a śrāvaka; if all these merits were combined and made complete, only then would they constitute the merit of a single pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, suppose all sentient beings in as many Buddha-worlds as there are sands in the Ganges were each to possess the complete merit of a pratyekabuddha;
even when this is combined to form the merit of a single bodhisattva, the merit of that bodhisattva would still exceed that [total] beyond measure.

Suppose one were to attain the samādhi of the "Equal Accumulation of All Virtues" (sarvaguṇasamavasaraṇa). Even if all sentient beings filling the trichiliocosm were likewise made to attain this samādhi of the Equal Accumulation of All Virtues, and the merit of these beings' samādhis were combined into a single, unobstructed, flawless, and non-conceptual wisdom.
Therefore, Ghoṣila!
All such offerings made through wisdom as these, when gathered together, constitute a Dharma-sacrifice; the compilation of this merit results in one of the marks of a Great Man of the Tathāgata.

In this manner, each of the thirty-two marks is like this; when they are all thus perfected, they constitute the Tathāgata’s complete physical form, which no sentient beings can conceive. Therefore, it is called the inconceivable body of the Tathāgata, the mark of a hundred merits.

When the Buddha spoke these marks of a Great Man resulting from the merit of a hundred blessings, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; a great radiance shone universally throughout the world while celestial flowers rained down, and hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.

The devas and people of the world, marveling at this unprecedented occurrence, leaped for joy and, each with palms joined, paid homage to the Buddha. Raising their voices in praise, they addressed the Buddha together, saying:

"If a daughter of noble family should resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, she will obtain excellent benefit and infinite celebration; that she shall eventually attain such marks of a hundred blessings, fully and perfectly complete, means she has already surpassed Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, all śrāvakas, and all pratyekabuddhas."
"So be it, World-Honored One!
How wonderful, how wonderful it is that anyone should hear of this Samādhi of the Accumulation of All Virtues!"

To attain the benefits of a bodhisattva, even merely hearing this name makes its virtue difficult to equal, let alone for one who hears it, believes in it, rejoices in it, and practices it accordingly.

Should anyone maintain this samādhi wherever they travel, they will thereby protect the sentient beings of that land; wherever this sutra travels, that territory shall be reckoned as a place established by a Buddha.

Even if the worlds of the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were filled with fire, one would pass through them to seek the hearing of this Dharma and this sutra; having heard it, one shall then return to great peace.
The World-Honored One said:
"So it is, so it is! O Devaputra!"
It is exactly as you have said.
Suppose there were someone who, upon hearing of this samādhi, did not believe or rejoice in it, and was unable to hear or receive it because they were held fast by Māra.
If there is a bodhisattva who does not manage to hear this samādhi, nor receives, upholds, recites, or explains it, I do not call such a person one of "much-hearing wisdom."
The devaputra addressed the Buddha:
"Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, through the holy intent of the Tathāgata, has established this Dharma, so that it may be proclaimed everywhere in future generations."

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted light from the mark between his eyebrows and from the mark of his topknot. This light shone universally throughout immeasurable and boundless Buddha-worlds. Following the radiance, a voice spontaneously issued forth, uttering this eulogy:
"The Tathāgata has already established this Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"It will not be long before I enter parinirvāṇa; only three months remain.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Ānanda.
"Having already provided this encouragement, I entrust you with this sutra; you should receive and uphold it, and explain it in detail for the sake of the various assemblies.
If there are people or bodhisattvas who study and maintain this samādhi, for those individuals, the Buddha shall not pass into parinirvāṇa and the Dharma shall not perish."
Why is this so? Ānanda, whoever receives and practices his Dharma sees the Buddha.
If one expounds and discusses it for the sake of the assembly, this constitutes the protection of the Dharma.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, shedding tears, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
I pray that you will remain for one kalpa, and even beyond one kalpa, out of great compassion, great pity, and great concern for the welfare and peace of the worlds of gods and humans.”
The World-Honored One said:

"Ānanda! Cease your grief and do not be sorrowful. Did I not tell you before that where this Dharma is fully present, the Buddha eternally abides, and one is likewise never separated from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones?"
Why is this? One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of form, nor by means of the marks and signs; if one perceives this Dharma, then one sees the Buddha.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Saṃdhinirmocana, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Vimalatejas, and all the other bodhisattvas;
the venerable Ānanda and the great śrāvakas;
and the entire assembly, including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, humans, and asuras.
All were filled with joy and bowed their heads in prostration.
